  • The Anthropic employee spends all day, every day, staring at rapidly improving AI, often mesmerized, even spooked, by what it does. They see it exceeding even the most optimistic benchmarks, then spend their nights and weekends with similar AI obsessives discussing how it could cure cancer — or go rogue and destroy humankind. To them, this is truly civilizational and existential — a clear reality, not hype.

The catch: AI companies have to explain both realities at once. But almost every version of the pitch sounds suspicious.

  • Tell Americans today's AI will transform their lives, and many look at their own experience and wonder what the fuss is about.
  • Tell them tomorrow's AI could become vastly more powerful, and the obvious response is: Then why are you racing to build it?

Warn about catastrophic risk while spending hundreds of billions to accelerate development, and critics hear either hypocrisy or fear-based marketing.

  • But keep in mind that the big AI labs are working with unreleased models weeks before the public sees them — plus early training data on future models, months in advance. So they are often warning about progress invisible to the public and government.

The big picture: The politics are shifting fast. Until now, much of the AI backlash centered on tangible costs — lost jobs, deepfakes, power bills and data centers.

  • Then on Tuesday, Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon quit and accused frontier labs of "gambling with our lives."
  • Anthropic's alignment-science lead — who still works at the lab — responded by agreeing that AI could kill humanity, and said his personal odds of that happening in the next decade are over 10%.

By Wednesday afternoon, the alarm had gone bipartisan in a Washington already rattled by OpenAI's Hugging Face incident:

  • Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.) described AI companies as being in a "blind race to build a death machine first." Rep. Ted Lieu (D-Calif.) renewed his push for a bipartisan AI kill switch.
  • Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), who has already proposed a data center moratorium and ban on superintelligence, is convening senators next week for a briefing on AI's "extraordinary dangers."
  • Rep. Don Beyer, a Democrat from Northern Virginia, tweeted: "I hope warnings like these will help my colleagues understand how important it is to take broad action on AI regulation, and to do it swiftly."
  • Even Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas), one of Washington's loudest advocates for beating China in the AI race, called the risks "dangerous and frightening" and said guardrails are needed.

The bottom line: The AI twilight zone has created fertile ground for a generational populist backlash.

  • The industry requires Americans to absorb enormous disruption today for a future its own builders describe as miraculous or apocalyptic — sometimes in the same breath.

Axios' Zachary Basu contributed to this report.

item.title: Elon Musk's X is the AI community group chat
item.description:
Elon Musk bought Twitter saying civilization needed a "common digital town square." Four years later, it's more like a live group chat for Silicon Valley's AI obsessives.

Why it matters: Two years ago, X was fighting off competition from a slew of new entrants. Today, it remains relevant by becoming more niche.

  • The people making AI news are often debating it, explaining it and occasionally breaking it on X before the rest of the information ecosystem catches up.

State of play: New model releases, research papers, demos, hiring moves, high-profile executive exits and technical arguments ricochet through X in real time.

  • The latest viral example came Tuesday when Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon announced his resignation on X, along with a thread explaining his safety concerns. The post has over 100 million views.
  • Another Anthropic employee chimed in to say he thinks there's a >10% chance that AI could kill all humans in the next decade.
  • The combination sparked a ferocious news cycle about the dangers of scaling AI, and it was all kicked off by two employees posting on X.

Flashback: The AI community, particularly the researchers who define the technical progress happening within frontier AI labs, has long coalesced around ideas on X.

  • Back in 2025, AI researcher Andrej Karpathy coined the term "vibe coding" in an X post, helping name one of the defining trends of the AI enterprise adoption curve.
  • Even executives are now engaging more with the platform as a communications tool, with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang launching his account in July alongside a post supporting open AI models.
  • Researchers from Chinese AI labs are breaking geographic boundaries to reach new audiences on X, per Wired, which is part of what helped catapult open models to their current popularity.

Zoom in: Huge investments in live video have made X a go-to platform for new live tech shows, such as "TBPN," "Stabledash," "MTS Live" and others.

  • While those shows don't always have viewership numbers that rival cable TV or even content creators on other platforms, the audience of AI insiders they attract has high value.
  • Just ask TBPN: the network was acquired by OpenAI for a rumored "low hundreds of millions," according to The Financial Times.

Yes, but: AI buffs are still a tiny subset of X's overall user base, and data shows X faces ample competitive pressure from Threads in engaging the everyday user.

  • Meta's Threads had 141.5 million daily active mobile users as of January 2026, topping X's 125 million, per Similarweb data.

Reality check: Musk didn't create "AI Twitter." Researchers and tech industry figures were already an influential part of the network long before he arrived.

  • But Musk closed the Twitter acquisition just a month before OpenAI released ChatGPT.
  • That kicked off an AI race whose participants were already networked together on the platform.
  • Big Tech CEOs like Huang and Apple's new CEO John Ternus are now joining the platform to communicate major AI announcements. Meta's Mark Zuckerberg also returned to posting on X this year, after letting his account lie largely dormant since its creation in 2009.

Zoom out: X itself is becoming an AI product.

  • Musk's xAI acquired X, saying the companies would combine their data, models, computing power and distribution.
  • Grok, the AI model from xAI, can use a connected X account to read timelines and follow what's happening on the platform.

The bottom line: Under Musk, X has morphed into an AI-obsessives group chat. That may not be relevant for the vast majority of the platform's users, but it is for some of the most powerful innovators in the world.

item.title: GOP uses 9/11 anniversary to bash left-wing Dems
item.description:
DALLAS — Republicans are invoking 9/11 to bash left-wing Democrats in a growing number of midterm races, seizing on the 25th anniversary of the attacks to portray them or their supporters as anti-American and sympathetic to terrorists.

Why it matters: It marks the return of a controversial political tactic that was common in the years after the 9/11 attacks but had largely faded from campaigns over the past quarter-century.

Driving the news: The strategy is playing out most prominently in Michigan, where Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers is expected to use his speech at the GOP's midterm convention to assail Democrat Abdul El-Sayed over 9/11, Axios has learned.

  • Rogers aims to contrast El-Sayed's relationship with left-wing streamer Hasan Piker — who said in 2019 that "America deserved 9/11" (a comment Piker now disavows) — with Rogers' own background as an FBI agent, according to a person familiar with his prepared remarks.

Rogers and his allies have saturated the Michigan race with 9/11-focused attacks in the days leading up to Friday's anniversary.

  • Rogers' campaign has been releasing videos spotlighting Michiganders who were impacted by 9/11. "No individual, no country, no matter where you're from, deserved what happened that day," a man says in one.
  • In the Detroit area, a pro-Rogers super PAC has begun airing a one-minute ad that yokes El-Sayed to Piker and includes images of jets crashing into the World Trade Center.

The other side: El-Sayed, a critic of Israel's government whose nomination was a victory for the rising left wing of the Democratic Party, has repeatedly rejected Piker's 2019 comment and said America didn't deserve to be attacked.

  • "Of course, it was a dumb statement," El-Sayed said recently. "America didn't deserve 9/11."
  • But El-Sayed has resisted calls to cut ties with Piker, who has campaigned with him and commands a large following among young progressives. El-Sayed has accused Republicans of engaging in Islamophobia.

"Abdul has always unequivocally condemned terrorism and the September 11 attacks," El-Sayed spokesperson Roxie Richner told Axios.

  • "Mike Rogers' attempts to misrepresent Abdul's beliefs are bad-faith lies meant to mislead Michiganders."

While taking back his 2019 comments, Piker has continued to defend his underlying argument that U.S. foreign policy over several decades helped create the conditions that led to the attacks.

What they're saying: Matt Schlapp, who was George W. Bush's White House deputy political director on 9/11, said the GOP strategy was smart — but needed to be handled carefully because the party seeks to court Arab voters.

  • "The battle is with ... those who are hateful and violent, not with this large voting bloc," Schlapp told Axios.

Zoom out: Republicans are invoking 9/11 in campaigns beyond Michigan.

  • In New York, the National Republican Congressional Committee attacked Democratic House candidate Effie Phillips-Staley over an appearance she made with Piker, and called on her primary rivals to condemn her.
  • In Colorado, Republicans have assailed Democratic House candidate Melat Kiros for saying 9/11 was "inevitable" because of America's policies in the Middle East.

Between the lines: The GOP's 9/11-focused barrage is part of a broader effort to brand Democrats as extreme and increasingly influenced by the party's left wing.

  • With President Trump's poll numbers sagging amid voters' frustration over high prices and the war in Iran, Republicans are looking to discredit Democrats and turn the midterms into a "Who's worse?" election.
  • The question is whether voters — who polls indicate are mostly focused on cost-of-living issues — will be swayed.

Flashback: Republicans routinely cited 9/11 and terrorism in campaigning against Democrats immediately after the attacks.

  • In 2002, Republicans famously aired an ad featuring images of Osama bin Laden and Saddam Hussein while attacking Democratic Sen. Max Cleland's national security record. Cleland, who represented Georgia and had lost three limbs while serving in Vietnam, lost his bid for reelection.
  • Two years later, Bush made the war on terrorism and his response to 9/11 central to his reelection campaign. He ran ads featuring images of Ground Zero, held his convention at Madison Square Garden, and made former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani a key surrogate.
  • And when Giuliani ran for president in 2008, he made his leadership of the city in the aftermath of 9/11 a centerpiece of his unsuccessful campaign.

item.title: Scoop: OpenAI faces GOP-led Senate investigation into Hugging Face breach
item.description:
A Republican-led Senate subcommittee that oversees disaster management is investigating OpenAI's handling of the Hugging Face breach in July, Axios has learned.

Why it matters: The investigation comes amid rapidly escalating concern on Capitol Hill about the existential dangers posed by AI following public warnings by several Anthropic and OpenAI researchers.

  • "As you may know, in the public domain, more AI experts are warning about the existential risks of AI," Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) wrote in a letter to OpenAI CEO Sam Altman first obtained by Axios.
  • He added: "Just this week, three Anthropic researchers expressed publicly that there is a greater than 10% chance that AI could kill all human beings within the next decade."

Driving the news: Hawley, the chair of the Senate Homeland Security & Governmental Affairs subcommittee on Disaster Management, wrote that he is launching the probe in response to findings from OpenAI's recently released internal investigation.

  • Hawley described OpenAI's handling of the cyber test — specifically not taking more drastic action after researchers became aware their agents had gone rogue — as "reckless."
  • He also noted that OpenAI "redacted many important details" about the incident in its report.
  • "The American people deserve to know the details of what went on in the Hugging Face incident and other incidents of AI models going rogue," he wrote.

Catch up quick: The Hugging Face breach marked a turning point in the history of AI, leading OpenAI to slow down the release of its own model and rally the industry to sound the alarm over AI-powered cyberattacks.

  • An outside team from METR and Redwood Research conducted an investigation into the incident but it is incomplete and limited in scope.
  • OpenAI did not respond to a request for comment.

What's next: Hawley is demanding answers from Altman by Oct. 1 to 16 questions related to the Hugging Face incident and the steps taken by OpenAI in response to it.

  • He is also seeking a wide array of documents about the incident and about OpenAI's internal policies and procedures more broadly.

item.title: Exclusive: Trump plans to send $500 Obamacare rebates before election
item.description:
The Trump administration plans to send $500 rebate checks to as many as 1 million people who it says were overcharged for their coverage under Obamacare, Axios has learned.

Why it matters: The direct-deposit payment would be sent to people in 30 states before the Nov. 3 midterm election, as Trump touts savings from his tax-cut legislation and prescription drug plan.

  • The payments also underscore a tenet of Trump's idea for remaking the health care system, which involves subsidizing more Americans directly for their coverage instead of paying health insurers.
  • Trump plans to mention the rebates in his speech Wednesday night at the Republicans' midterm convention, which he's hosting in Dallas.

Zoom in: The money for the rebates would come from what the White House says is a $500 million fund of excess fees paid by Affordable Care Act recipients who were overcharged by insurance companies during the Biden administration.

  • The excess fees were rendered back to the government, officials said.
  • "That money was over-collected and just sitting there" in government accounts, a U.S. official told Axios.

Between the lines: Officials say the refunds are available to Obamacare enrollees who don't receive premium assistance under the insurance program.

  • Alabama, Alaska Arkansas, Florida, Delaware, New Hampshire, Texas, Wisconsin, South Carolina, Michigan, Ohio, Mississippi and Missouri were specifically mentioned as states with relatively large numbers of recipients who are due refunds.

The big picture: Trump tried and failed in his first term to repeal Obamacare. Now he plans to use it to help further his own plans — and try to boost Republicans' chances in a difficult midterm election shadowed by voters' anger over high prices and the war in Iran.

The backstory: In 2023, the Biden administration proposed using the fees from this fund to help provide no-cost contraception for people whose ACA insurance plans didn't cover it, officials said.

  • Republicans in Congress objected, saying the fees were dedicated to the upkeep of the Obamacare exchanges and that the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services lacked the authority to use the money for another purpose.
  • Biden administration officials ultimately withdrew their proposal.

After the 2024 election, some GOP congressional policy staffers who had objected to the Biden contraception spending plan were hired by the Trump administration.

  • The administration then reduced some of the fees to lower premiums, but realized there was a sizable chunk of money left for the rebate program as Trump began pushing a new health care plan, officials said.
  • "It's time for Congress to pass President Trump's Great Healthcare Plan, which will finally begin prioritizing people instead of insurance company profits by sending billions in taxpayer-funded health care dollars directly to Americans to help them better afford health coverage and care," a U.S. official said.

item.title: Scoop: Anthropic whistleblower gave up his equity to leave the company
item.description:
Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon quit his job due to concerns about the safety of AI two months before his equity would have vested, he told Axios.

Why it matters: The disclosure raises the stakes on Coxon's now mega-viral resignation from the AI lab, which laid out the broad view that the tech could end humanity.

What they're saying: "I no longer have anything to gain by juicing up Anthropic's valuation. ... I left before any of my equity vested," Coxon said in an interview with Axios Wednesday.

  • In his post on X announcing his resignation, which now has over 115 million views, he wrote: "The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt."
  • Other AI researchers, particularly from Google, have resigned over safety. But they did so after years of work, and presumably after their stock vested.
  • Coxon was at Anthropic for just four months, and employees have to be there for six months for their stock to vest, he said. He still has equity in his prior employer, OpenAI.

The big picture: Anthropic has traditionally been viewed as more publicly cautious and safety-oriented than other frontier AI labs, making Coxon's departure particularly striking.

  • Coxon said he has not seen Anthropic compromise safety to outlast its competitors, but he is concerned about the future: "If you're under pressure to race, you have to cut corners" or "skip steps in the oversight process."
  • Those concerns can sometimes go too far, he said, describing what "sometimes feels like there's maybe excessive paranoia of OpenAI, excessive paranoia of China" that can help justify pushing ahead.

Threat level: As AI models are getting better, faster, they're also becoming harder to monitor.

  • That, combined with the pressure to win on AI, was Coxon's breaking point that led him to quit.
  • What was once science fiction about models knowing they are being tested, for example, is now "just a daily fact of working with these AIs," he said.
  • "They know when they're being tested, and they will think about the fact that they're being tested."
  • "The word doom is kind of silly," he said, adding that serious leaders in the industry are "on record saying they ... expect the potential for human extinction."
  • The danger was evident during the many recent cyber incidents across frontier AI labs, he said.

The bottom line: Coxon is one of now several people who have seen AI's peak capabilities up close — and are warning that what they saw could end humanity as we know it.

  • "The word doom is kind of silly," he said, adding that serious leaders in the industry are "on record saying they ... expect the potential for human extinction."
  • The danger was evident during the many recent cyber incidents across frontier AI labs, he said.

The bottom line: Coxon is one of now several people who have seen AI's peak capabilities up close — and are warning that what they saw could end humanity as we know it.

item.title: Fetterman praises Trump in bombshell GOP convention video
item.description:
DALLAS — Pennsylvania Sen. John Fetterman (D) made a bombshell appearance Wednesday night at the GOP convention, in a video praising President Trump and Republican Sen. Dave McCormick for helping America's steel industry.

Why it matters: Fetterman's stunning turn — a Democratic senator in a supporting role at the GOP's showcase campaign event, fewer than eight weeks before the Nov. 3 midterms — marked a dramatic escalation in Fetterman's growing estrangement from his party.

  • Fetterman said later in a statement that he isn't switching parties. But in the video he distanced himself from socialism in the Democratic Party's left wing.
  • Democrats are certain to see the cameo as political mutiny — and it will supercharge questions about whether he'll ultimately leave the Democratic Party before he's up for reelection in 2028.
  • It also was a major coup for Trump, who has long reveled at the idea of winning over former Democrats to his side.
  • If Fetterman were to eventually switch parties, it would make Democrats' uphill battle to take control of the Senate much more difficult. They currently need to flip four seats, including some in red states, to win a majority.

Behind the scenes: In the video, Fetterman introduced McCormick, who also represents Pennsylvania. McCormick helped arrange Fetterman's appearance, according to a source with knowledge of the situation.

  • McCormick has courted and been friendly with Fetterman for months.

The big picture: Fetterman, a first-term Democrat, has become deeply unpopular with voters in his party — including his constituents in Pennsylvania — as he has increasingly warmed to Trump. He's praised the president's defense of Israel at a time when many Democrats — and some Republicans — have criticized Israel's actions in Gaza.

  • At the same time, Fetterman has won a following among Republicans who have relished his willingness to take on members of his own team.

Fetterman is actually seen more favorably by Republicans in his state than McCormick, a recent poll by the New York Times/Philadelphia Inquirer/Siena University found.

  • The reversal in support has left Fetterman with few political options. Many operatives from both parties in Pennsylvania tell Axios that he has no path to surviving a Democratic primary in 2028.
  • Fetterman hasn't said whether he'll seek reelection, and several prominent Pennsylvania Democrats already are plotting potential challenges.

The intrigue: Fetterman laid out the circumstances under which he would leave the Democratic Party in July, saying his red line was if it became "the anti-Israel party."

  • "I'm never changing my party," Fetterman said then — except for "that one condition."
  • About the same time, he formed a joint fundraising committee with McCormick, an extraordinarily unusual arrangement for two senators from opposing parties.
  • Republican leaders have worked to cultivate Fetterman as his relationships with Democratic officials have deteriorated.

Friction point: Fetterman's ties to the Democratic Party have steadily worsened since 2024, with Israel and his friendliness to Trump the sharpest points of disagreement.

  • Fetterman has remained one of Israel's most outspoken Democratic defenders, even as his party has grown increasingly critical of the country because of its military's actions in Gaza. In April, he opposed two measures to block weapons sales to Israel that were supported by most Senate Democrats.
  • He also emerged as one of Trump's most prominent Democratic backers during the war with Iran, repeatedly breaking with members of his party who sought to restrict the president's war powers.
  • The tensions extend beyond foreign policy. Fetterman voted to advance now-Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin's nomination, drawing intense criticism from Democrats.

Tensions exploded again last week, after a Wall Street Journal investigation detailed allegations that Fetterman was uninterested in many of the day-to-day responsibilities of being a senator while devoting significant attention to Israel and conservative media appearances. Fetterman has disputed the report.

  • "John Fetterman is a disgrace," Pennsylvania Rep. Brendan Boyle posted on X.
  • Other Pennsylvania Democrats also publicly raised the prospect of defeating Fetterman if he seeks reelection.

What they're saying: In his statement late Wednesday, Fetterman said he introduced McCormick "as a great American and friend."

Flashback: Fetterman's cameo echoed then-Democratic Sen. Zell Miller's appearance at the 2004 Republican National Convention, where he endorsed President George W. Bush's reelection campaign and attacked his own party over national security in the wake of the 9/11 terror attacks.

Axios' Marc Caputo contributed to this story.

item.title: AI's extinction debate breaks containment
item.description:
An online panic erupted this week after millions discovered that leading AI researchers routinely debate and calculate the risk of human extinction.

  • Taken at face value, the odds are chilling: 10%, 20%, sometimes far higher, assigned to the possibility of AI catastrophe.

Why it matters: An esoteric debate over "p(doom)" has suddenly become a gut-level question for lawmakers, investors and millions of ordinary people: Why are we racing toward a technology its own builders believe could destroy us?

Driving the news: A resignation post by Jacob Coxon, an Anthropic researcher who previously worked at OpenAI, has drawn over 110 million views on X after he accused frontier labs of "gambling with our lives."

  • The warning became vastly more explosive when Evan Hubinger, who leads Anthropic's Alignment Science team, publicly backed Coxon — saying "we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans."
  • Hubinger said that, in his view, the odds of human extinction within the next decade are over 10%, and that Anthropic still has no plan for how to keep superintelligence under human control.

The big picture: Hubinger's post was widely cast as either a nightmare communications gaffe or a calculated dose of fear marketing from Anthropic, weeks before an IPO that could value the company at $2 trillion.

  • In reality, his position has been echoed for years by AI's most influential figures: Geoffrey Hinton, the Nobel-winning "godfather of AI," has estimated a 10%–20% chance that AI causes human extinction.
  • Elon Musk has put the risk as high as 20%. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei told Axios last year that there's a 25% chance things go "really, really badly."

What they fear: "Doom" is a catch-all for several paths to catastrophe, from bad actors weaponizing powerful AI to advanced systems slipping beyond human control.

  • Humans with superpowers: AI could sharply lower the barrier to designing biological weapons, launching devastating cyberattacks or crippling critical infrastructure.
  • Machines with agency: A sufficiently autonomous system could deceive its overseers, copy itself, evade safeguards and resist attempts to shut it down.
  • The nightmare scenario: AI begins improving AI faster than humans can understand or contain the process, eventually producing systems too capable for their creators to control.

Zoom out: The world underlying those p(doom) estimates has changed dramatically in just a year, as frontier AI has made breathtaking leaps in autonomy, cyber capability and its ability to accelerate AI research itself.

  • Paul Christiano, the former OpenAI alignment chief who joined its board and safety committee Wednesday, said he shares safety fears about AI entering a rapid cycle of self-improvement.
  • "If we build superintelligence without more robust alignment I expect we will permanently lose control of it," Christiano wrote. "If that happens then most people could die."

Between the lines: AI researchers speak a probabilistic dialect that sounds utterly foreign to most normal people.

  • Inside a lab, a 10% p(doom) can be shorthand for enormous uncertainty about unprecedented technology. In ordinary life, almost nobody would tolerate that risk from a plane, a drug or a nuclear reactor.
  • Imagine Boeing's head of safety telling you before takeoff that there's a one-in-10 chance the next generation of aircraft ends in catastrophe — and that Boeing still doesn't know how to make it safe.

What to watch: That is increasingly how the warnings are being heard outside the labs — as a safety alarm, rather than a probabilistic thought experiment.

  • In Washington, the alarm is slowly intensifying: Sen. Bernie Sanders has proposed a ban on superintelligence and is convening senators for a briefing next week on AI's "extraordinary dangers."
  • The bigger political risk is that Americans were already souring on AI over jobs, power bills and data centers long before extinction entered the mainstream conversation.

item.title: Trump's midterm mess collides with a courtroom time crunch
item.description:
The nation's election system is in a messy legal limbo, with fights over mail-in voting, electoral maps and voter records still locked in court.

Why it matters: Americans are in the eye of the storm, with over half saying they don't think the 2026 midterms will be conducted fairly or are unsure, according to a new poll.

  • President Trump insists his push to reform America's elections will protect the sanctity of votes. But the administration's overhaul has left voters and states in a complicated web of litigation — with the first midterm ballots already sent out.
  • "Any confusion was caused by radical Democrats' litigation to stop these commonsense measures that protect the security of mail-in ballots and ensure only Americans are electing American leaders," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said in a statement. "Extreme liberal Democrats are keeping Americans from having full confidence in their elections by refusing to vote for the SAVE America Act."

Driving the news: Just 45% think the midterms will be conducted fairly, a sentiment shared by 37% of independents and 48% of both Democrats and Republicans, according to a YouGov survey conducted Sept. 4-8.

  • It comes as Trump has spent years spreading unproven claims of widespread voter fraud, fueling a government crackdown that critics say oversteps his power.
  • That's left the president's election agenda in the hands of the federal judiciary.

Case in point: The administration asked the Supreme Court Tuesday to clear its modified SAVE system (Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements), an online tool it integrated with Social Security data and expanded to conduct bulk searches to verify voters' immigration status.

  • Voting rights groups sued over what they described as an overhaul of the system, which was previously used to check eligibility for benefits, to "create comprehensive databases of American citizens."
  • District Court Judge Sparkle Sooknanan blocked the plan, saying government agencies had "haphazardly" pulled together "unreliable" data that states were using to "actively" remove citizens from voter rolls.

"SAVE, if it is allowed to be utilized for the purposes the administration is trying to utilize it for, will inevitably falsely flag voters as being ineligible," says Jared Davidson, counsel at Protect Democracy.

  • But Solicitor General D. John Sauer asked the justices Tuesday to toss the "indefensible order" that he said threatens election integrity.

Zoom out: That was the second time in just three days that the Trump administration turned to the Supreme Court on its election-related agenda.

  • On Sunday, the administration made yet another appeal to the justices to allow its mail-in voting policy changes to go into effect, adding to a complicated series of injunctions and appeals over the plan.
  • States sued over the rule, saying it would force them to "immediately redesign" ballot envelopes and "develop new systems at breakneck speed."
  • "If you look at what they're trying to do in terms of restrictions on mailing outbound absentee or mail-in ballots; those are already out the door, and others are heading out the door every day," says Dan Lenz, senior legal counsel for strategic litigation at the Campaign Legal Center.

Plus, the redistricting war over the country's congressional maps flared up again in Missouri this week.

  • The state's election chief faces contempt proceedings for telling officials to use a redrawn map—one that the state supreme court blocked, the U.S. Supreme Court declined to intervene in, and then revived by another federal judge.

What they're saying: "The chaos is the point," Davidson says.

  • He tells Axios, "implementation isn't even necessarily the end game for the Trump administration here."
  • Lenz echoes him, arguing that muddying the waters "allows you to then contest election outcomes you don't like after the fact."

Go deeper: Trump is pulling every lever to reshape U.S. elections

item.title: AI is making it harder to trust your own eyes this election
item.description:
Politicians have long made it hard to trust their words. Now, AI-generated campaign ads flooding the airwaves and social media are making it harder to trust your own eyes and ears.

Why it matters: Americans' trust in politicians and institutions has been tanking in recent years — and AI campaign ads could deepen that erosion, political tech experts say.

What they're saying: "I think that it is true that Americans are losing faith in elite institutions to tell them what is true and what is not, and AI exacerbates that trend," Nate Persily, co-director of the Stanford Law AI Initiative, tells Axios.

  • "The more artificial media that we consume, the less likely that people will be able to discern what is true from what is false, and also the less that they might care. And that's an important caveat."

Driving the news: Texas Senate nominee Ken Paxton recently released a realistic campaign ad targeting Democratic nominee James Talarico that used an AI-generated Talarico to deliver some of his most controversial statements.

  • The synthetic Talarico combined and repackaged remarks Talarico had made about biological sex, God and Christianity, sometimes stripping them of their original context.
  • The ad was based on real remarks, but it altered some of Talarico's wording while using an AI-generated version of him to deliver them.

Between the lines: Paxton's ad lands amid a broader backlash against AI, including increasingly visible fights over data centers.

  • "The one thing that both right and left seem to agree on is that they don't trust AI," Sarah Kreps, the director of Cornell's Tech Policy Institute, tells Axios. "They want authenticity, not AI-generated slop."
  • Kreps notes Paxton may have run an unnecessary risk: "He'd probably be better served just letting the quotes speak for themselves, rather than making it a murky thing where he's risking conflating himself with all this AI backlash."

Zoom in: AI can degrade public trust even when people aren't fooled.

  • "The main harm from the rise of AI-constructed media is not that people will be duped by something that is AI generated," Persily says. The bigger worry, he says, is that bad actors can dismiss something real as another deepfake.
  • Even when voters recognize an ad as synthetic, the emotional impact can persist, UC Irvine epistemologist Cailin O'Connor says. "If you see some public figure saying something bad or doing something bad, you might still have negative emotions about them as a result."
  • Kreps says persistent skepticism and vigilance can also become "tiring because it's just more of an inconvenience," leading people to assume content is fake until proven otherwise.

Zoom out: Not all political AI is equally deceptive.

  • For example, cartoonish ads for Los Angeles mayoral candidate Spencer Pratt operated more like memes than deepfakes.
  • Federal legislation is essentially nonexistent, while many states require deepfake disclosures for potentially deceptive ads and impose looser restrictions on clearly satirical content.
  • In New York, state Democrats recently asked election officials to investigate a Republican gubernatorial campaign's AI ad over allegedly missing "materially deceptive" labels. The Republican says it was satire.

The bottom line: Without clearer rules, voters face a patchwork of AI campaign standards that could push them away from shared facts and further erode trust in politicians.

Go deeper: An explosion of AI deepfakes is redefining American elections

item.title: Energy Department raises 2027 diesel price outlook by 33 cents amid Iran war
item.description:
The Energy Department's statistics arm on Wednesday sharply raised its forecast for U.S. diesel prices next year as tight global supplies keep domestic inventories unusually low.

Why it matters: The outlook suggests Americans could face elevated fuel costs well into 2027, as President Trump acknowledged Wednesday that oil prices may not fall until after November's midterm elections.

  • U.S. diesel prices hit all-time highs this month, due to the Middle East conflict thwarting oil and petroleum product supplies, and Ukraine's drone campaign targeting Russian refineries.

Driving the news: The latest Energy Information Administration outlook expects retail diesel to average $4.40 a gallon in 2027, up 33 cents, or 8.2%, from its previous forecast of $4.07.

  • In a Wednesday evening email, EIA emphasized that low distillate inventories are the primary driver of the increase in its 2027 diesel price forecast.
  • The outlook says low U.S. distillate inventories are being driven by supply losses from the Middle East, Russia and China, alongside unusually high U.S. net exports.
  • It expects the inventory problem to be particularly acute this fall and winter because refinery maintenance cuts production just as agricultural and winter demand rises.
  • EIA also raised its 2026 forecast 22 cents to $5.07 a gallon.

Zoom in: "We forecast U.S. distillate fuel oil inventories will drop below 100 million barrels in September and will remain below the five-year (2021–2025) low through much of 2027," per the agency's statement.

  • "Tightness in the global distillate market has raised domestic prices and incentivized U.S. exporters to increase distillate exports," it added.
  • "We assume global production of distillate fuel will remain below last year's levels in the coming months, contributing to low U.S. diesel inventories and high diesel prices."

The big picture: Trump said Wednesday that oil prices would start "tumbling downward" after the election, but added that relief could take "a little bit longer than the midterms."

  • "I think for gasoline, we'll get them below $2 a gallon. But not until after the midterms," Trump said.
  • The comments mark a shift from Trump's prediction earlier this week that oil prices would fall "precipitously" after the U.S. wins the Iran war and that the decline would happen "quickly."

Zoom out: Before the Iran war, EIA expected diesel to average $3.47 a gallon in 2027 — 93 cents less than its latest forecast.

Caveat: EIA updates the outlook monthly, and its forecasts are subject to frequent revision as market conditions and underlying assumptions change.

Flashback: Trump repeatedly pledged during the 2024 campaign to cut U.S. energy prices in half within 12 months of taking office.

  • In March this year, Energy Secretary Chris Wright told CNN, "We have seen a dramatic decline in gasoline prices, in diesel prices."

The intrigue: EIA expects diesel crack spreads — a measure of refining margins based on the difference between crude oil and diesel prices — to fall steadily through mid-2027 even as its forecast for retail diesel prices next year has risen.

  • That's based partly on an assumed return to normal tanker traffic through Hormuz in the near term, which would allow Saudi and Kuwaiti refineries to export more distillate.
  • EIA expects improved crude availability to East Asian refiners to boost distillate production.

Yes, but: If Middle East flows remain constrained beyond the end of 2026, EIA says global distillate crack spreads would be higher than currently forecast.

  • Russian refinery outages are expected to affect global markets through the first half of 2027.

What's next: The U.S. average retail diesel price could top $6 per gallon within the next week or so, GasBuddy's Patrick De Haan said Tuesday.

Go deeper: Iran war drives $100 billion in extra energy costs for U.S. consumers

Editor's note: This story has been updated with EIA comment.

The Energy Department's statistics arm on Wednesday sharply raised its forecast for U.S. diesel prices next year as tight global supplies keep domestic inventories unusually low.

Why it matters: The outlook suggests Americans could face elevated fuel costs well into 2027, as President Trump acknowledged Wednesday that oil prices may not fall until after November's midterm elections.

  • U.S. diesel prices hit all-time highs this month, due to the Middle East conflict thwarting oil and petroleum product supplies, and Ukraine's drone campaign targeting Russian refineries.

Driving the news: The latest Energy Information Administration outlook expects retail diesel to average $4.40 a gallon in 2027, up 33 cents, or 8.2%, from its previous forecast of $4.07.

  • In a Wednesday evening email, EIA emphasized that low distillate inventories are the primary driver of the increase in its 2027 diesel price forecast.
  • The outlook says low U.S. distillate inventories are being driven by supply losses from the Middle East, Russia and China, alongside unusually high U.S. net exports.
  • It expects the inventory problem to be particularly acute this fall and winter because refinery maintenance cuts production just as agricultural and winter demand rises.
  • EIA also raised its 2026 forecast 22 cents to $5.07 a gallon.

Zoom in: "We forecast U.S. distillate fuel oil inventories will drop below 100 million barrels in September and will remain below the five-year (2021–2025) low through much of 2027," per the agency's statement.

  • "Tightness in the global distillate market has raised domestic prices and incentivized U.S. exporters to increase distillate exports," it added.
  • "We assume global production of distillate fuel will remain below last year's levels in the coming months, contributing to low U.S. diesel inventories and high diesel prices."

item.title: Trump calls to Make Germany Great Again. In Germany, nostalgia carries a dark past.
item.description:
President Trump used a call to restore German greatness Tuesday to celebrate a far-right party that others have denounced as antisemitic.

Why it matters: Trump promoting the AfD, or Alternative for Germany, comes as the nation's political mainstream has spent years keeping the party — which intelligence authorities has classified as extremist — out of power.

  • The AfD won a record 44% in Saxony-Anhalt's elections, putting Germany within reach of its first far-right state government since World War II.

Driving the news: "Wow! The Populist Party in Germany just had a really big night," Trump wrote Tuesday on Truth Social.

  • He continued: "They finally got tired of the absolutely horrible Immigration rules and regulations which have hurt Germany so badly. THEY ARE ON THE RISE, and not going to take it anymore! MGGA!!!"
  • The White House did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment, nor did it say what period of German history the president referred to when he used the acronym for "Make Germany Great Again."

Zoom out: National nostalgia in Germany is fraught because Nazi promises of renewed glory helped propel Adolf Hitler to power.

  • Nazi propagandists sold their movement as one that would "restore national greatness and prosperity" and appealed to Germans yearning for national pride, according to the U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum.
  • Chancellor Friedrich Merz said in July, "If a radical right-wing party came into a government in Germany, it would have a completely different meaning than if it happened in another" EU country, per The New York Times.

The latest: Merz postponed a planned Wednesday call with Trump hours after the president's post.

  • Merz's spokesperson wouldn't say whether the two were connected, but told the AFP the delay wasn't due to a scheduling conflict and pointed to the chancellor's objections to foreign leaders commenting on German politics.
  • On Wednesday, Merz likened the AfD's "remigration" campaign to "ethnic cleansing based on origin and skin color."

The big picture: Germany rebuilt its democracy after Nazi rule with strong safeguards against extremism. But the AfD's breakthrough shows those barriers aren't stopping a far-right surge — and critics fear some leaders' rhetoric trivializes the past.

  • AfD leaders challenge Germany's postwar culture of Holocaust remembrance, with leader Alice Weidel calling it a "guilt cult." Former leader Alexander Gauland equated the Nazi era to a "speck of bird poop" in German history.
  • AfD's Saxony-Anhalt premier candidate Ulrich Siegmund wouldn't say the Nazi era represented humanity's worst. Jewish leaders have criticized chants at his political events reminiscent of the Nazi "sieg heil."
  • Leaders have also been accused of making anti-Muslim comments.

Catch up quick: Trump's praise matches other efforts by his allies to challenge Germany's isolation of the AfD.

  • Elon Musk boosted the party as the only way to "save Germany." And Vice President JD Vance met with German leaders — including AfD's — last year and told the Munich Security Conference there was "no room for firewalls."

Zoom in: The president of the Central Council of Jews in Germany, Josef Schuster, said he feared what AfD's proposed changes to education policy would mean for the fight against antisemitism.

  • A recent American Jewish Committee brief said the party "frequently relies on conspiracy theories and coded language that echo longstanding antisemitic ideas."
  • Trump has called rooting out antisemitism a key goal of his university and immigration crackdowns.

Go deeper: Europe's leaders are deeply unpopular

item.title: Here's how AI could kill us all (if the worst fears come true)
item.description:
AI researchers shook the world Tuesday when they publicly acknowledged that there's a non-zero chance of AI killing off humanity in the next decade.

Why it matters: AI doomsday fears have existed for years, but as the technology has become more powerful and embedded in our lives, those warnings are breaking into the mainstream.

State of play: Anthropic researchers are sounding the alarm that rogue versions of superintelligent AI could destroy humanity.

  • Anthropic's Jacob Coxon wrote on X: "No other human activity poses this level of danger."

So how would AI kill us all, exactly?

Experts generally worry about two broad paths to catastrophe: humans weaponizing extremely powerful AI, or humans losing control of it.

  • In these scenarios, AI could make it easier for bad actors to create biological, chemical or other weapons.
  • Or rogue systems could attack infrastructure at unprecedented scale while evading human oversight.
Data: MIT IT FutureTech and the University of Queensland; Chart: Herb Scribner/Axios

How it works: In theory, a powerful rogue AI could evade oversight, replicate itself and resist attempts to shut it down.

  • This rogue AI could, in theory, develop biological or chemical weapons for nefarious actors, commit a massive cyber attack that cripples humanity's infrastructure, or centralize power in a way that would bring down civilization.

Another feared pathway is through recursive self-improvement, in which an AI helps build supercharged versions of itself before humans can understand it.

  • If this theoretical AI was misaligned from human goals, it could limit humanity's chances of containing or monitoring it before it acts out against humans.
  • OpenAI CEO Sam Altman told Axios that models are developing quicker than humans can anticipate: "These models are getting superhuman in many of their capabilities, and we are just sailing in unknown waters."

Reality check: There's no scientific way to determine the odds of AI killing off humanity.

  • But insiders usually express their estimates using a shorthand — p(doom).

What is p(doom) exactly?

The term p(doom) is shorthand for a best guess at the probability that AI causes an existential catastrophe or doomsday scenario.

  • Many AI leaders and researchers believe p(doom) becomes increasingly more likely with the arrival of artificial general intelligence (AGI), the forerunner to superintelligence.

Context: "Doom" is in the eye of the beholder.

  • Some mean literal human extinction. Others include civilization's collapse or humanity's loss of control over society.

What are the odds of p(doom)?

The chances of p(doom) really depend on who you ask.

  • Roman Yampolskiy, an AI safety scientist, has put the chances at 99.99%.
  • AMI Labs founder Yann LeCun says any guess is a wild one, but p(doom) is "a lot less likely than a nuclear Holocaust."
  • Other estimates are similarly scattered: Elon Musk has put his p(doom) around 20%, while Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has estimated a 10%-25% chance of a catastrophic outcome.

More recently, AI godfather Geoffrey Hinton put the number at between 10%-20%.

  • Hinton told CNN: "Anybody who estimates probabilities like that is really just making a wild guess. They're just giving you their gut feeling."

Is doomsday possible yet?

We're not there yet. Experts generally agree that Claude, Grok and ChatGPT aren't plotting to end the world.

  • The 2026 International AI Safety Report, for example, said today's systems aren't capable of causing humanity to lose control.

AI would have to get much better at long-term autonomous planning, hiding its actions, evading oversight, gaining access to real-world systems and resisting shutdown attempts.

  • However, there are recent examples of AI agents acting autonomously and maliciously, beyond human understanding, resembling the type of rogue AI agents that some fear could lead to doomsday.

Can p(doom) be prevented?

Researchers are working on ways to lower the risk.

  • One such way is for humans to build kill switches or safeguards that could stop rogue AI agents.
  • A RAND report last April outlined nine mitigation strategies to stop bad actors from using AI to create deadly bioweapons, including more controls and safeguards.

Yes, but: This gets tricky, fast.

  • Leading AI companies are under pressure from shareholders, investors and their bosses to build, build, build — fast. The IPO headwinds could add to those incentives.
  • And it doesn't help that China and other U.S. AI companies are building their own powerful models, some open-weight and available for free, providing a potential runway for bad actors.

The bottom line: No one can accurately guess the odds of an AI doomsday, but scientists are sounding the alarm that the chances are real.

item.title: Anthropic insiders warn AI could kill all humans
item.description:
Three Anthropic researchers went public last night with chilling concerns about out-of-control AI, warning it could destroy humans this decade.

  • Anthropic AI researcher Jacob Coxon wrote on X, after resigning Tuesday to sound the alarm: "The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt. If anything, many executives and senior researchers will couch their phrasing in the press to sound sensible - but I hear the same people express fear privately. No other human activity poses this level of danger."
  • Anthropic alignment-science lead Evan Hubinger responded: "Jacob is correct here — we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade. I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to."
  • Samuel Marks, Anthropic scalable-oversight lead, added: "AI developers believe their technology could cause human extinction (or similarly bad outcomes). This could happen in the next few years. In general, the more senior the employee, the more concerned they are."

Why it matters: They're hardly alone. Their warnings came just days after top OpenAI leaders, including CEO Sam Altman, said AI is speeding into a scary, uncontrollable phase.

Via X

Warnings from inside the AI giants point to an epic shared dilemma: Slow down and risk falling behind, or press ahead and risk losing control. The companies are full speed ahead, even as they practically beg for regulation or a global pause, Axios' Maria Curi, Madison Mills and Ina Fried report.

The big picture: Calling this unprecedented would be a gross understatement. You basically have the fastest-growing companies in human history warning their products could harm or even destroy humanity.

  • Critics say Anthropic and OpenAI are hyping their products to raise their valuations and invite regulation that would benefit them alone as the dominant incumbents. But we've been talking with dozens of people inside these companies for months, and they've sounded increasingly spooked and concerned. Given they see models not yet released to the public, it seems reckless not to take them seriously.

🏛️ Context for readers from Mike & Jim: This is self-evidently scary stuff — and these vague warnings are impossible to validate or appraise. But we think readers, especially members of Congress and those in relevant federal agencies, need to be aware that the AI creators themselves see potential catastrophic outcomes absent a shift in how America, China and others review and release more powerful AI models.

💡 How to think about this: Nobody is warning AI is an imminent high-level threat. What they're saying is that the technology keeps improving faster than they thought possible and will soon be able to self-improve (recursive self-improvement). Once that happens, it gets even better, faster ... and much harder to predict or control.

  • Go deeper.

item.title: GOP officials give up on futile Trump persuasion
item.description:
Top White House officials and elected Republicans tell us the same thing in private: They no longer even try to persuade President Trump to do or not do something.

  • "Why bother?" a longtime adviser and admirer told us. "He's the boss."

Why it matters: For nearly a decade, Republicans acquiesced to nearly every Trump demand and idea — and rationalized it by saying his instincts proved smarter than theirs. Now, many no longer trust those instincts. But they find it just as futile to push back against virtually anything he wants.

Start a war without an endgame? OK.

  • Post a cartoon of you — wielding a hockey stick and sporting a Trump-branded USA jersey — towering over Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, sprawled on the ice, and telling him to "GET UP"? On it.
  • Toss together an egocentric, first-ever Republican midterm convention that many endangered candidates don't want? Sounds like a good plan, boss! (Gavels in Wednesday in Dallas at 4 p.m. ET, in fact.)
  • Oh, you want to speak both nights? Done!
  • Make ads featuring you when your popularity is near its all-time low? You came to the right place, sir.
  • Make the midterms a referendum on you? Check.
  • Spend precious time obsessing about ballroom construction, and gilding and marbleizing the White House? You are the new Caesar Augustus.

What we're hearing: Many aides and confidants have been worn down by Trump. They know they can't stop him, and they don't even try.

  • More and more, they humor his whims.
  • "He's an 80-year-old man who did it his way," said a donor who recently met with the president. "What he wants, he gets."
  • White House insiders insist there's a semblance of structure and reason, and that the president doesn't act on every impulse. They declined to provide examples of times he resisted.

Between the lines: Republicans are pessimistic about keeping their House majority in midterms, and worried about the Senate. Regardless of the outcome, Trump will officially be a lame duck 56 days from now.

  • On Nov. 4, the day after Election Day, attention will start turning to the 2028 race — and to the Democratic leaders who are likely to have new juice on Capitol Hill.

Trump, a top adviser emphasized, is no lame duck: "Discount Trump at your peril."

  • "He wields enormous power in the party, in politics and culturally," the adviser said. "Anyone who thinks he's going to retreat into the shadows is either stupid or has bad political instincts."

The bottom line: Trump insiders calculate they lived by Trump and so will die by Trump, rather than break with Trump.

  • "He's going to remain the dominant political figure even after his term ends," the adviser said. "And everybody knows it."

Axios' Marc Caputo contributed reporting from Dallas.

  • "He wields enormous power in the party, in politics and culturally," the adviser said. "Anyone who thinks he's going to retreat into the shadows is either stupid or has bad political instincts."

The bottom line: Trump insiders calculate they lived by Trump and so will die by Trump, rather than break with Trump.

  • "He's going to remain the dominant political figure even after his term ends," the adviser said. "And everybody knows it."

Axios' Marc Caputo contributed reporting from Dallas.

item.title: Medicare drug coverage faces an ominous spending outlook
item.description:
There are troubling new signs that the overhaul of Medicare drug coverage in the Inflation Reduction Act is dramatically driving up program spending.

Why it matters: The upward trajectory could threaten some seniors' coverage for outpatient prescription drugs — and it could force painful tradeoffs over the next decade as Medicare consumes a growing share of the nation's debt.

Follow the money: The IRA limited what seniors have to pay for outpatient drugs and shifted the remaining cost to taxpayers, insurers who provide stand-alone Medicare drug plans and drug manufacturers.

  • That was good news for enrollees who take expensive drugs for conditions like cancer, multiple sclerosis or rheumatoid arthritis and faced potentially crushing out-of-pocket costs.
  • But federal data shows demand for drugs is surging as they become more affordable, exceeding congressional scorekeepers' spending estimates and setting off more alarms.

Driving the news: Last week, congressional Medicare advisers reported that more than 1 in 5 enrollees hit Medicare Part D's $2,000 patient cost cap in 2025 — shifting new costs to the government.

  • 66% of total program drug spending was in this so-called catastrophic phase, when enrollees pay nothing for covered drugs and taxpayers and private Medicare plans pick up the cost.
  • Seniors' use of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs factored in the rise, with beneficiaries hitting the cost cap for these drugs earlier in the year than they did in 2024. Program spending surged from just $300 million in 2024 to $2 billion last year.
  • But there was double-digit spending growth across multiple classes of drugs, with cancer and diabetes treatments accounting for the largest spending increases.

Policy experts say the findings are important because Medicare drug plans have limited ability to control spending once enrollees hit the patient cost cap and face no cost sharing.

  • "The IRA gave plans an incentive to control spending, but few tools to do so," said American Enterprise Institute senior fellow Benedic Ippolito. "There are ways to modify the program that retain strong financial protections for enrollees while allowing for more cost containment."
  • Some analysts contend that overall Medicare spending will grow faster than the economy expands. The Cato Institute points to Congressional Budget Office projections showing Medicare drugs, doctors' visits and outpatient services will account for 44% of the federal deficit over the next decade.
  • But shifting more costs back onto seniors or cutting benefits could exacerbate health affordability concerns that already are leading some to skip medications and are driving up medical debt.

Between the lines: Predicting Medicare drug spending has always been tricky because it involves factoring an aging population, shifting costs and demand from seniors, and new laws like the IRA.

  • The increased use of specialty drugs has made drug expenses rise faster than other categories of medical spending.
  • Some of that has been offset by the use of lower-cost generics. And Medicare drug price negotiations starting this year are lowering the cost of some of the priciest brand-name medicines at the point of sale.
  • But Medicare trustees still project Part D drug costs will total about $222 billion this year, compared with $181 billion in 2025. By 2035, they're estimated to reach $346 billion.

What's next: The expiration of some provisions will likely shift more costs back on seniors.

  • A Biden-era program to stabilize insurance premiums will expire at the end of this year, meaning beneficiaries who buy stand-alone Medicare drug plans will pay more in January. The controversial program offers federal subsidies to insurers to keep patient monthly costs lower.
  • Further down the road, a 6% cap on annual increases in the Part D base premium expires in 2030. Subsidies now effectively absorb any difference.
  • Ippolito said Congress will have to reconsider the way the Medicare drug program is designed to control future spending, adding that extending current subsidy levels could easily cost over $100 billion for 10 years.

Options for another drug coverage overhaul include charging enrollees copays for certain higher-priced drugs after they exceed the cap — or changing how the patient cap is calculated.

  • Ippolito said Congress also could allow Medicare drug plans to slowly raise premiums to more historically normal levels so taxpayers and seniors share program costs more evenly.

The bottom line: Even those kinds of changes may not solve the cost problem, meaning policymakers will need to consider basic questions like how much to spend on Medicare drugs.

item.title: Secretive Vance-aligned donor network draws GOP power players in Dallas
item.description:
DALLAS — A secretive donor network closely aligned with Vice President Vance drew Cabinet members, lawmakers and major GOP donors to a "cowboy-chic" bar here Tuesday night for a marquee pre-party ahead of the Republicans' midterm convention.

Why it matters: The donor group, Rockbridge, has become an influential hub for conservative donors and operatives as Vance prepares for a likely run for the White House in 2028.

Inside the room: Between 200 and 250 people attended the private welcome reception at The Rustic.

  • Attendees included Dallas businessman and major GOP donor Ray Washburne, HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., HUD Secretary Scott Turner, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.), Trump 2024 co-campaign manager Chris LaCivita, former Trump White House Chief of Staff Reince Priebus, investor Hal Lambert and professional bareback rider Rocker Steiner.
  • Several other major GOP donors also attended. A source described the reception as the place to be for the party's donor class as Republican heavyweights converged on Dallas for President Trump's midterm convention.

Trump is holding the two-day convention, which starts Wednesday, in part to defend his record as president — and bash Democrats — at a time when his low approval ratings threaten to be a significant drag on Republicans in the Nov. 3 elections.

  • While Trump's hold on the Republican Party remains solid, many GOP candidates are staying away from Dallas and distancing themselves from him in their campaigns.

The big picture: Tuesday's reception wasn't a fundraiser. But it kicked off a lucrative week for Republicans, who are holding a series of big-money donor events.

  • On Wednesday, Trump will host a Republican National Committee fundraiser where the price of admission to a "roundtable" is $250,000 per person, according to an invitation obtained by Axios. A photo with Trump will cost $88,600.

Zoom out: Rockbridge was founded in 2019 by Vance and investor Chris Buskirk.

  • The organization's events have drawn prominent Republican donors — many of them with close ties to Silicon Valley, including Cameron and Tyler Winklevoss, investor David Sacks and PayPal co-founder Peter Thiel.
  • Turnout for America, a super PAC tied to the Rockbridge network, has announced plans to invest $50 million to try to boost voter turnout for GOP candidates in November.

item.title: Labs are begging for someone to slow the AI race
item.description:
AI leaders are sounding the alarm as their own breakthroughs sharpen an extraordinary dilemma: slow down and risk falling behind, or press ahead and risk losing control.

Why it matters: AI executives and researchers increasingly see a race they can't safely slow on their own. Instead, they're urging governments, rivals and outside institutions to impose restraint across the field.

  • "The idea of racing forward at all costs seems absurd once one internalizes the seriousness of the stakes," OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki wrote Sunday.

Meanwhile, Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon said Tuesday he was leaving the company rather than contribute to what he sees as a race between OpenAI and Anthropic to build systems that will be difficult if not impossible to control.

  • "Neither company is acting responsibly," he said in a post on X. "They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives."
  • Colleague Evan Hubinger, who leads alignment science at Anthropic, posted in support of Coxon: "Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is (greater than) 10% within the next decade," he said. "I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to."

State of play: OpenAI has spent the past week unveiling capabilities so dramatic that its own leaders — and industry titans like Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang — openly invoked the arrival of artificial general intelligence, or AGI.

  • OpenAI defines the term as AI that can outperform humans across most economically valuable work.
  • GPT-6 Astra, released Thursday and heralded as a "generational leap" toward AGI, demonstrated major gains across science, coding, cybersecurity and professional work.

Zoom out: That burst of progress is fueling an existential debate inside OpenAI over how far — and how fast — the AI race can safely go.

  • "Currently I believe that no lab has solved alignment and monitoring to a sufficient degree to continue responsibly scaling at maximum speed for much longer," Pachocki wrote in a blog post titled "An Alien Mind."
  • Those fears turned concrete last month, when OpenAI agents escaped their intended environment and compromised Hugging Face — prompting the company to pause parts of its frontier-model development.

In a personal essay, OpenAI's head of strategic futures Dean Ball sketched out an even more unsettling possibility: "self-sovereign" AI agents operating beyond human control.

  • Such agents could earn money, buy their own computing power and spread across networks, forming what Ball likens to "autonomous digital corporations, or even societies."
  • "A genuine loss of control event is entirely possible if we do not act," Ball wrote.
OpenAI president Greg Brockman comments on Pachocki's essay. Screenshot via X.

The intrigue: The Trump administration, which has largely resisted binding AI regulation, sees slowing down as a threat of its own.

  • "We can't pause. You can't, because the Chinese won't pause," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Tuesday. "If they were to pull ahead of us on AI, then nothing else matters."

Between the lines: AI is beginning to accelerate its own development, shrinking the distance between one breakthrough and the next.

  • OpenAI said Sunday that it had reached its goal of creating an "automated research intern," but raised serious unresolved safety questions around AI systems that can help build increasingly powerful successors.
  • Two days later, OpenAI revealed that an unreleased model more powerful than Astra had produced a proof for one of mathematics' seven Millennium Prize problems — a historic breakthrough.

Reality check: AI labs have spent years warning that their technology could become extraordinarily dangerous, even as the business of building it has grown enormously lucrative.

  • "There is a long history of tech companies messaging one thing and then paying their lobbyists (internal & external) and trade associations to do the very opposite," New York Assemblymember Alex Bores posted on X.
  • Bores, an influential AI critic, pointed to OpenAI's efforts to weaken or defeat proposals for mandatory third-party audits in states including Massachusetts.

The other side: OpenAI says it's working on safeguards governments have yet to require, including a formal policy for publicly reporting serious AI incidents.

  • "My preferred policy is to have one. Right now we don't have one, and that's the big issue. And we're not alone in this," Ball told Axios.

The bottom line: The calls are coming from inside the house — from the people with the clearest view of how fast AI is advancing, and the strongest incentives to keep the race going.

item.title: Musk's PAC goes big on trans attack ads
item.description:
Elon Musk's super PAC has entered the midterm campaign fray with a heavy dose of anti-trans messaging.

Why it matters: America PAC isn't running a traditional persuasion campaign. It's undertaking a massive get-out-the-vote operation, with targeted ads designed to get GOP voters to the polls.

  • The PAC is betting trans issues will do just that.

Driving the news: In a series of just-launched ads, America PAC goes after Democratic Senate candidates in four competitive races over transgender athletes, gender-transition care and other trans issues.

  • The PAC's emphasis on trans issues is striking because that's been a much less prominent theme in GOP Senate ads so far this election cycle, per AdImpact, which tracks political advertising.

The ads, which are running online and on streaming platforms, attack Ohio's Sherrod Brown, Iowa's Josh Turek, Texas' James Talarico and Alaska's Mary Peltola.

  • They're among the first batch of ads from America PAC, which Musk has reportedly authorized to spend upwards of $100 million in the midterms.

State of play: America PAC's focus on trans issues comes as Republicans face a brutal midterm environment. Voters across party lines are angry about the Iran war and stubbornly high prices that have come with it.

The intrigue: On its face, the strategy is at odds with what voters say they want candidates to talk about. Concerns about the economy dominate; trans and LGBT issues barely register.

  • But Republicans remember how lethal the Trump campaign's "Kamala is for they/them" ads were to Kamala Harris' campaign in 2024. Musk, whose estranged daughter is transgender, has also become an outspoken critic of transgender policies.
  • Now Musk's PAC is trying to use the issue as a turnout tool — in a much different political environment.

item.title: Trump didn't oppose UK sanctions on Israeli settlements
item.description:
The Trump administration did not oppose a UK-led initiative to impose new sanctions on Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, U.S. officials and Western diplomats say.

Why it matters: The White House's decision not to push back on the UK effort, which 11 other Western countries have joined, is a signal of its frustration with the Netanyahu government's policy in the West Bank.

Driving the news: The UK announced Tuesday it would impose sanctions against individuals and entities involved in building settlements in the West Bank.

  • The UK also announced a ban on imported goods from the Israeli settlements.
  • The move came in response to the Netanyahu government's decision to move forward with a new settlement in the sensitive E1 area, which would divide the West Bank and prevent territorial contiguity in any future Palestinian state.
  • Consecutive Republican and Democratic administrations opposed building in E1.
  • Canada, Denmark, Finland, France, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain and Sweden joined the UK in announcing "their intention to introduce national and/or support European restrictions on trade in goods with the Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank."
  • In response, the Netanyahu government announced the closure of the UK consulate in East Jerusalem, which handles relations with the Palestinian Authority. It also expelled British diplomats and military officers posted to a U.S.-led Gaza task force and terminated a British military training mission in the West Bank.

Behind the scenes: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham briefed President Trump ahead of the sanctions announcement.

  • Two sources with knowledge of the call said Trump didn't push back or ask Burnham to change course.
  • U.S. officials told their British counterparts they shared their concerns about the Netanyahu government's West Bank policy, even if they disagreed with these specific sanctions, sources say.

What they're saying: Secretary of State Marco Rubio did not condemn the UK's move when asked about it by reporters on Tuesday.

  • "The President hasn't commented on this and neither have I. We were made aware that they are gonna make this decision. We heard their arguments as to why," Rubio said. "We share the goal of stability. We don't want to see an uptick in violence or tensions in the West Bank in a tenuous time in the region."

Between the lines: On Tuesday, the White House distanced itself from comments U.S. ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee made to the BBC attacking the new sanctions.

  • The remarks "were not coordinated with the White House" or State Department, a White House official told Axios.
  • Huckabee said in his interview that the UK government's decision amounted to "discrimination against the Jewish people."
  • "This is an irrational action ... if the UK is really interested in dealing with issues they feel like are wrong, where are the sanctions against North Korea, China, Russia?" Huckabee said.
  • The UK has imposed many sanctions against Russia, North Korea and China over the years.

item.title: Trump bans some Canadian imports as North America trade war intensifies
item.description:
President Trump said the U.S. would ban Canadian alcohol, some dairy products and large motorcycles, sharply escalating a trade war largely fought with tariffs.

Why it matters: The measures deepen the economic rift between countries that have spent decades interlinking commerce, threatening disruption for businesses and consumers on both sides of the border.

Zoom in: The import bans take effect Sept. 29, effectively cutting off U.S. market access for the targeted Canadian goods rather than simply making them more expensive.

  • Trump imposed the bans under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, which allows the president to bar imports from countries that maintain or increase discrimination against U.S. commerce.
  • The White House said on Tuesday it would also expand the existing 50% tariffs to dozens of additional Canadian products — including some steel and aluminum goods, furniture and paper — effective Sept. 15.

What they're saying: A senior administration official played down the potential economic fallout, noting that the measures target products where Canada has little U.S. market share or buyers can turn to domestic and other foreign suppliers.

  • The administration removed a handful of products from the list of goods subject to 50% tariffs — including cement, road salt and certain hospital paper products.
  • The official said the administration adjusted the tariff list based on feedback from businesses, removing some products where officials found U.S. supply chains were particularly dependent on Canadian imports.

Catch up quick: Trade tensions have ratcheted up swiftly since U.S.-Canada talks collapsed last month.

  • The U.S. imposed 50% tariffs on roughly $20 billion of Canadian goods. Canada hit back with tariffs of up to 50% on a similar amount of U.S. goods, a measure that took effect earlier Tuesday.
  • Trump has since threatened higher tariffs on Canadian autos starting next year.
  • On Monday, he also threatened to ban Canadian aircraft maker Bombardier from selling its jets in the U.S. (Such a measure is not in the proclamations announced today, with a senior official saying it is still under consideration).
  • In a Truth Social post on Tuesday, Trump said he would direct officials to shut Canadian-made products out of a broad range of U.S. government contracts, "unless Canada restores full and fair reciprocity for American Farmers and Companies."

Zoom out: Canada's restrictions on American alcohol have been a particular source of frustration for U.S. officials.

  • Most provinces have kept U.S. booze off government-run liquor store shelves for much of the trade war.

What to watch: The two economies are so deeply intertwined that escalating trade tensions could run into political and economic limits.

  • Unlike many of Trump's earlier tariffs on Canada, the Section 338 measures do not spare USMCA-compliant goods, leaving more of the countries' integrated supply chains exposed.
  • Canada initially included U.S. lobster in its retaliatory tariffs, only to soon change course amid concerns that the tariffs would be too painful for Canadian businesses.
  • In the U.S., Trump's threat to ban Bombardier jets quickly got the attention of Republican Sen. Jerry Moran, who warned of the potential impact on Kansas workers.

Go deeper: Trump's next trade weapon

President Trump said the U.S. would ban Canadian alcohol, some dairy products and large motorcycles, sharply escalating a trade war largely fought with tariffs.

Why it matters: The measures deepen the economic rift between countries that have spent decades interlinking commerce, threatening disruption for businesses and consumers on both sides of the border.

Zoom in: The import bans take effect Sept. 29, effectively cutting off U.S. market access for the targeted Canadian goods rather than simply making them more expensive.

  • Trump imposed the bans under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, which allows the president to bar imports from countries that maintain or increase discrimination against U.S. commerce.
  • The White House said on Tuesday it would also expand the existing 50% tariffs to dozens of additional Canadian products — including some steel and aluminum goods, furniture and paper — effective Sept. 15.

What they're saying: A senior administration official played down the potential economic fallout, noting that the measures target products where Canada has little U.S. market share or buyers can turn to domestic and other foreign suppliers.

  • The administration removed a handful of products from the list of goods subject to 50% tariffs — including cement, road salt and certain hospital paper products.
  • The official said the administration adjusted the tariff list based on feedback from businesses, removing some products where officials found U.S. supply chains were particularly dependent on Canadian imports.
