item.title: A growing movement wants AI out of schools
item.description:
America's two largest school districts both imposed sweeping AI bans this past week, hitting the brakes on a technology that's rapidly making its way into classrooms around the country.

Why it matters: Research on AI's educational value is mixed. Some studies have found personalized AI tutors can improve learning, while other research has linked AI-assisted essay writing to weaker critical thinking.

Driving the news: New York City's public school district blocked AI use for roughly 600,000 students in Pre-K through 8th grade, restricting it to specific uses for high school students.

  • Hours later, Los Angeles Unified imposed a districtwide moratorium on AI use on school devices for the 2026-27 school year, following a separate screen-time crackdown.
  • And Chicago school board candidates are lining up to sign a pledge demanding a three-year moratorium on generative AI in its schools.

What they're saying: Nicki Petrossi, a mother and co-founder of the Tech-Safe Learning Coalition, tells Axios one parent called today's kids "the guinea pig generation," adding, "you won't find a parent who's not concerned about this."

  • Another parent told her that their "five-year-old, who still believes in the Tooth Fairy, [is] being asked to interact with chatbots. What could go wrong?"

Between the lines: Bans may be hard to enforce because AI is already embedded in classroom technology.

  • Google's Gemini, for example, can appear when students search on school Chromebooks.

The other side: Some educators warn sweeping bans could eliminate useful tools.

  • "If you're working with students with special needs or English language [learning] students...there are a lot of benefits to using technology that allow us to augment the lessons," Janice Jackson, executive director of the Aspen Institute Education & Society Program and former Chicago Public Schools CEO, tells Axios. "We shouldn't throw that out."
  • "The jury is still out on the quality of each policy, and that is not an indictment on any of these policies. It's more related to the fact that this is still very new," she says.

By the numbers: Teachers are worried AI is becoming an easy out for students, according to a recent NPR/Ipsos poll.

  • 55% say students mostly use it as a shortcut to avoid work, 54% say it makes critical thinking skills harder to build, and 57% say it makes it harder to gauge what students actually know.
  • More than half say their school hasn't given them guidance on how to handle AI.

The bottom line: "The ed tech industry has a reckoning coming," Brendan Bouffard, associate general counsel at Fairplay, adding that multiple states are considering strong legislative guardrails.

  • "It's going to be good to see some real standards put in place to help make sure that these tools are being used safely and effectively for students, and that these tech companies are actually held accountable for what they're selling."

Go deeper: Schools adopting AI could see benefits (and more work) - Axios Kansas City

item.title: AfD just won 44% in a German state. Now Germany's firewall faces its biggest test.
item.description:
Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) won a record 44% in Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday, leaving a small party with seats that could determine whether it can lead the nation's first far-right state government since World War II.

Why it matters: Germany rebuilt its democracy after Nazi rule with unusually strong safeguards against extremism. AfD's breakthrough shows those barriers aren't stopping Europe's far right from becoming dominant electoral forces.

The latest: AfD more than doubled its 20.8% share in 2021, hitting its highest vote share ever in a state election and finishing ahead of the center-right CDU at 17%.

  • BSW, the party that hasn't ruled out working with the AfD, barely cleared the 5% threshold parties need for parliamentary representation.
  • Together, AfD and BSW would hold 43 seats, one more than a majority.
  • BSW, a populist party, combines far-left economics with far-right migration policies and calls for closer ties to Russia.

Yes, but: The arithmetic may not be enough.

  • BSW co-chair Amira Mohamed Ali said Sunday the party would neither vote for AfD's Ulrich Siegmund nor CDU Premier Sven Schulze. Instead, she wants a nonpartisan premier who would govern with BSW and AfD.
  • This would require support from AfD, but Siegmund rejected the idea.
  • Siegmund suggested Sunday he may persuade some lawmakers to switch parties to help him secure a majority.

Catch up quick: AfD has won the most votes once before, in 2024, but it has never governed.

  • In 2024, it finished first in Thuringia, marking the first far-right victory since World War II, but other parties kept it out of government. Sunday's result is AfD's strongest.

Flashback: Trump allies' support for the far-right party became a transatlantic flashpoint during Germany's 2025 federal election.

  • Elon Musk boosted the AfD on X, saying "only the AfD can save Germany," and he appeared by video at an AfD campaign rally.
  • Vice President JD Vance met with AfD's leader just before that election and told the Munich Security Conference there was "no room for firewalls," a reference to mainstream parties' stance against governing with the AfD.

Between the lines: Saxony-Anhalt's intelligence service has classified the state AfD as a right-wing extremist organization.

  • Siegmund, AfD's 35-year-old candidate for Saxony-Anhalt's premier, has drawn scrutiny over his treatment of Germany's Nazi past.
  • At AfD events, an emcee has shouted "Sieg!" and supporters answered "Mund!" — splitting his surname into a call-and-response that the head of Germany's Central Council of Jews says evokes Nazi chants.
  • Siegmund declined to call the Holocaust humanity's worst crime, saying he would not presume to rank all crimes.

The big picture: Europe's far right is moving in sharply different directions.

  • Hungary's Viktor Orbán lost power after 16 years this spring, yet Italy's Giorgia Meloni leads the country's longest-serving uninterrupted postwar government.
  • In France, far-right National Rally leader Marine Le Pen is the early front-runner for the 2027 presidential election.

Context: Germany's postwar system was built in the shadow of the Nazis' destruction of the democratic Weimar Republic.

  • The 1949 Basic Law embraces the concept of a "militant democracy" to defend against movements that seek to abolish the constitutional order.

What's inside: The AfD laid out a program for how it would use state power:

  • Rewrite the mandate of the state intelligence service that investigated the party.
  • Allow homeschooling, give the government greater control over which textbooks schools can use and end its public broadcasting agreement with neighboring states.
  • Create a deportation task force.
  • Require state-funded organizations to demonstrate a "patriotic basic attitude."

What we're watching: German officials, including the defense minister, have floated limiting intelligence sharing over concerns about AfD's ties to Russia.

item.title: Exclusive: Latino leaders push Beshear on Texas' race for governor
item.description:
Dozens of Latino lawmakers and leaders are pressuring Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, who chairs the Democratic Governors Association, to invest $10 million in the Texas governor's race, according to a letter to Beshear that Axios obtained.

  • Texas state Rep. Gina Hinojosa, who polls suggest is running a strong challenge to Gov. Greg Abbott (R), is trying to become Texas' first Latino governor. Beshear must decide soon how to invest the DGA's cash in the 36 states with governor's races in November.

Why it matters: Beshear is considering a presidential run in 2028. Latino voters are critical in the early primary states of Nevada and New Mexico, and are a key swing vote in general elections.

  • Beshear's decision on where to spend tens of millions in DGA money this fall is an early test of his political instincts — and whether he can carry out an effective campaign strategy without making enemies that could cost him in a 2028 primary.

Zoom in: The signees of the letter — which include Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego, a potential rival of Beshear's in the presidential primary — wrote that "not investing in Texas would not only send a message to Latino voters in 2026, but it sends a message to Latino voters heading into 2028."

  • "No other candidate in recent history has come this close to winning the Governor's Mansion in Texas, and we are proud that it is now a Latina that made this a close race, but unfortunately, she has done so without real investment from DGA," the letter says of Hinojosa.

There are 36 state governors' races this fall, including several in 2028 swing states such as Wisconsin, Michigan, Nevada and Georgia. And then there's Texas, where a Democrat hasn't won a statewide race in three decades.

  • It's unclear how much money the DGA has for the November elections, but in the last midterm cycle, 2022, the DGA spent about $170 million.
  • Texas is one of the most expensive states to campaign in, and Democratic leaders in Washington have been skeptical about flipping the state blue.
  • Abbott, who is running for a fourth term as governor, has $67 million cash on hand compared with Hinojosa's $3 million, according to the latest finance report in July. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report labels the race "likely" Republican.
  • Even so, most recent polls show Abbott with less than 50% support and Hinojosa within 5 points.

What they're saying: "While there will certainly be more investment, announcing a figure would only advantage the [Republican Governors Association] in any counter-investment. I look forward to working with the signees of the letter in supporting Gina," Beshear told Axios in a statement.

  • He said Hinojosa "has proven herself to be a great candidate" and that the DGA is "currently investing by paying expenses and recently providing staff."
  • DGA communications director Sam Newton added: "As the race in Texas becomes increasingly competitive in the final stretch, we will be ready to capitalize on any opportunity to make a real difference."

Zoom out: The letter to Beshear is also signed by several members of Congress from Texas, including Rep. Greg Casar, chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, and Rep. Joaquin Castro.

  • They argued that an Abbott victory wouldn't affect just Texas but the U.S. House of Representatives.
  • They wrote that Abbott will further gerrymander the state and take away up to 10 more Democratic-held congressional seats over the next four years.
  • "The only way to stop it is to elect Gina Hinojosa as governor of Texas, who has promised to veto illegal maps," they wrote.

Between the lines: As the DGA's chair, Beshear would have some advantages if he were to launch a White House run. He's building relationships across the country and glad-handing many potential donors.

  • The potential downside is that the DGA has limited resources and Beshear could wind up creating 2028 foes, depending on which races he invests in and which he doesn't.

item.title: Dem governors weighing White House face the DeSantis dilemma
item.description:
Top aides for Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis' failed 2024 presidential campaign have a warning for Democratic governors eyeing a 2028 run: Don't wait too long after November's midterms to jump into the race.

Why it matters: In the coming months, Govs. Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania, Wes Moore of Maryland, JB Pritzker of Illinois and Andy Beshear of Kentucky will face a dilemma similar to what confronted DeSantis after his 2022 reelection:

  • Do they get in the race early — before their postelection legislative sessions start — and risk not being focused on their constituents? Or do they wait until late spring to rack up policy wins and give their opponents a head start on a White House run?
  • Their allies and some of their teams are already debating which path to take, Democratic sources tell Axios.

Driving the news: Many DeSantis aides now regret how they handled the months between DeSantis' commanding reelection victory in November 2022 and his entry into the presidential race in late May 2023, several told Axios.

  • Donald Trump announced his reelection bid in November 2022 and began attacking DeSantis while the governor was scoring state policy wins and promoting a new book — but falling behind in the presidential race.

"In this atmosphere, you can't be president by just being a great governor and boasting about your legislative wins," said Ryan Tyson, a Republican pollster and president of the Tyson Group who was a senior adviser to DeSantis.

  • "That's how they did it in the '90s — not anymore. Enough of the voters in these early nomination contests will be driven by emotion more so than logic."

A former DeSantis aide added: "There were diminishing returns for DeSantis passing conservative legislation [in Florida's 2023 session] because of his preexisting, extensive record."

  • "I don't think it's very helpful for a Democratic governor waiting to announce for 2028 to use the legislative session to just keep doing more of what they've already been doing," the former DeSantis aide said.
  • "It would have to be new stuff to command media attention or fix a potential political vulnerability."

Reality check: The 2028 Democratic primary is different from the 2024 Republican primary.

  • DeSantis was running against a former president who was still extraordinarily popular with the GOP base.
  • The legal indictments against Trump led many Republican voters to rally around him.
  • Trump also made the unorthodox move to go negative against DeSantis in paid and earned media before the Florida governor got in the race.

Between the lines: If Democratic governors declare their candidacies before their legislative sessions are over, they could face attacks from rivals in the presidential race in addition to rebellions within their states.

  • Ambitious state legislators could hold up bills and criticize newly elected governors for focusing on national politics just months after winning reelection.

Axios asked Shapiro, Moore, Beshear and Pritzker if they had committed to finishing their state legislative sessions before declaring whether they were running for president.

  • None of them directly answered the question.
  • Shapiro spokesperson Manuel Bonder told Axios: "While we appreciate team DeSantis taking a break from banning abortion and rigging our democracy to offer unsolicited advice, I'll repeat what the governor has made clear: The midterms run through Pennsylvania, and the only thing we are focused on is winning up and down the ballot this November."

Top aides for Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis' failed 2024 presidential campaign have a warning for Democratic governors eyeing a 2028 run: Don't wait too long after November's midterms to jump into the race.

Why it matters: In the coming months, Govs. Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania, Wes Moore of Maryland, JB Pritzker of Illinois and Andy Beshear of Kentucky will face a dilemma similar to what confronted DeSantis after his 2022 reelection:

  • Do they get in the race early — before their postelection legislative sessions start — and risk not being focused on their constituents? Or do they wait until late spring to rack up policy wins and give their opponents a head start on a White House run?
  • Their allies and some of their teams are already debating which path to take, Democratic sources tell Axios.

Driving the news: Many DeSantis aides now regret how they handled the months between DeSantis' commanding reelection victory in November 2022 and his entry into the presidential race in late May 2023, several told Axios.

  • Donald Trump announced his reelection bid in November 2022 and began attacking DeSantis while the governor was scoring state policy wins and promoting a new book — but falling behind in the presidential race.

"In this atmosphere, you can't be president by just being a great governor and boasting about your legislative wins," said Ryan Tyson, a Republican pollster and president of the Tyson Group who was a senior adviser to DeSantis.

  • "That's how they did it in the '90s — not anymore. Enough of the voters in these early nomination contests will be driven by emotion more so than logic."

A former DeSantis aide added: "There were diminishing returns for DeSantis passing conservative legislation [in Florida's 2023 session] because of his preexisting, extensive record."

  • "I don't think it's very helpful for a Democratic governor waiting to announce for 2028 to use the legislative session to just keep doing more of what they've already been doing," the former DeSantis aide said.
  • "It would have to be new stuff to command media attention or fix a potential political vulnerability."

Reality check: The 2028 Democratic primary is different from the 2024 Republican primary.

  • DeSantis was running against a former president who was still extraordinarily popular with the GOP base.
  • The legal indictments against Trump led many Republican voters to rally around him.
  • Trump also made the unorthodox move to go negative against DeSantis in paid and earned media before the Florida governor got in the race.

Between the lines: If Democratic governors declare their candidacies before their legislative sessions are over, they could face attacks from rivals in the presidential race in addition to rebellions within their states.

  • Ambitious state legislators could hold up bills and criticize newly elected governors for focusing on national politics just months after winning reelection.

Axios asked Shapiro, Moore, Beshear and Pritzker if they had committed to finishing their state legislative sessions before declaring whether they were running for president.

  • None of them directly answered the question.
  • Shapiro spokesperson Manuel Bonder told Axios: "While we appreciate team DeSantis taking a break from banning abortion and rigging our democracy to offer unsolicited advice, I'll repeat what the governor has made clear: The midterms run through Pennsylvania, and the only thing we are focused on is winning up and down the ballot this November."

item.title: Witkoff and Kushner, in a first, visit Ukraine for peace talks
item.description:
President Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrived in Kyiv on Sunday for diplomatic talks aimed at resuming negotiations between Russia and Ukraine.

Why it matters: Kushner and Witkoff traveled to Kyiv right after talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow. This is Witkoff and Kushner's first trip to Ukraine despite months of negotiating with both sides and multiple trips to Russia.

  • Sunday also marked the highest-level visit by a U.S. official to Ukraine since Trump started his second term.

Driving the news: U.S. and Russian officials offered positive assessments of Kushner and Witkoff's three-hour meeting with Putin on Saturday.

  • "Kushner and Witkoff are making an effort, and we are making progress," a Russian official said.
  • A White House official said Witkoff, Kushner and Putin discussed "plans for next steps, which will be announced in the coming weeks."
  • Witkoff, Kushner and their team left Moscow on Saturday night, landed several hours later in Poland, and then traveled by land to Kyiv.

Zoom in: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky discussed Ukrainian preparations for continuing the war through the winter, a source familiar with the meetings said. Kushner and Witkoff stressed they want a breakthrough before winter, the source said.

  • Zelensky later confirmed that the possibility of the war continuing through the winter was discussed.
  • "We very much hope that we will be able to reach agreements with our American partners, and we are counting on the support of our European partners if the war continues in winter — and this is how it appears at the moment," he said.
  • Witkoff and Kushner met twice with Zelensky and his senior advisers. National security advisers from the U.K., France and Germany joined a third meeting.
  • After the second meeting with Zelensky, Trump's envoys said they were "encouraged by the substantive discussion" and looked forward to making more progress.

What they're saying: A second source who participated in Sunday's talks said the meetings "went well" and that Kushner and Witkoff want to work with the parties on a "refreshed" peace proposal.

  • "Things may move in a good direction if there's a follow-up by all parties involved," the source said.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details throughout.

item.title: Trump's energy boss wavers on gasoline price path
item.description:
Energy Secretary Chris Wright on Sunday cautiously predicted gasoline price relief is on the way, but stopped short of firm or precise pledges.

Why it matters: Pump prices are at their highest Labor Day weekend levels on record, and the midterms loom less than two months away.

  • His appearances on Sunday political shows also comes as diesel prices, which ripple through the economy, are at all-time highs.

"I think prices headed downward is — is not an unreasonable expectation," he said on CBS's "Face the Nation."

State of play: On that show and others, Wright noted that U.S. gasoline demand typically falls after Labor Day with the end of the traditional summer driving season.

  • He also promoted recent administration moves to ease some environmental requirements for summer gasoline blends.
  • "Gasoline production is about to go up and demand is about to go down. So, if I had to guess, they're more likely to go down than go up," Wright said on CNN's "State of the Union."

Catch up quick: U.S. regular gasoline prices averaged $4.15 per gallon Sunday, per AAA data.

Data: AAA; Chart: Ben Geman/Axios

The intrigue: Wright also pointed to declining prices for gasoline futures contracts in the months ahead.

  • "The marketplace thinks gasoline prices are going to move meaningfully lower. So trust the market, certainly don't trust my predictions.," he said on ABC's "This Week," per a transcript.

Yes, but: Futures prices months ahead are volatile, and they're not a crystal ball for what will be happening in retail markets.

  • Pump prices have climbed in recent weeks amid a flare-up in hostilities that has driven crude oil prices higher.
  • Crude oil is already at its highest level in roughly six weeks, with the global benchmark above $96 per barrel at Friday's close, even though more oil appears to have been transiting the Strait of Hormuz recently.

What we're watching: Oil prices could see another jump when markets open for the week, following fresh conflicts this weekend.

item.title: Witkoff and Kushner meet with Putin about ending Ukraine war
item.description:
President Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met with Russian President Vladimir Putin at the Kremlin Saturday and discussed U.S. ideas for ending the war in Ukraine.

Why it matters: Witkoff and Kushner want to resume direct talks between Russia and Ukraine after negotiations were suspended six months ago and the fighting has escalated ahead of winter.

  • Witkoff and Kushner, who are expected to travel to Kyiv on Sunday, got Russia and Ukraine to agree to a short pause in airstrikes to allow the trip to take place.

What they are saying: Putin told Witkoff and Kushner at the top of the three-hour meeting that he has "full trust" in the U.S. mediation between Russia and Ukraine.

  • Witkoff thanked Putin for releasing ex-U.S. Marine Robert Gilman and for agreeing to pause airstrikes against Ukraine while U.S. negotiators are visiting Kyiv.
  • Putin said the pause will begin at midnight Saturday Moscow time and noted that Ukraine also reduced its strikes.
  • "We will do our utmost to provide for the safety of the negotiations," Putin said.

Yes, but: Over the last several days, Russia dramatically increased its drone and missile attacks on Ukraine, including Kyiv and other major cities.

The big picture: The trip to Kyiv by Trump's envoys will be the highest-level visit by a U.S. official to Ukraine since President Trump started his second term.

The intrigue: Gene Lange, the acting sanctions czar at the Treasury Department, joined Witkoff and Kushner on the trip. Lange participated in a preparatory meeting with Putin envoy Kirill Dmitriev but didn't attend the meeting with Putin.

  • Lange's participation indicates that U.S. sanctions against Russia were part of the discussions.
  • Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent met his Russian counterpart on the sidelines of the G20 Finance Ministers meeting in Asheville, North Carolina last week and said the U.S. would not give Russia economic relief until it ends the war with Ukraine.

What they said: Yuri Ushakov, Putin's foreign policy aide, told Russian reporters afterward that Witkoff and Kushner "made serious preparations for this trip. They not only expressed their traditional interest in a speedy end to the fighting but also formulated a number of ideas regarding possible resolution paths."

  • A White House official said that "officials from the National Security Council, State Department, and Treasury Department" joined Witkoff, Kushner and Putin at the meeting. "The two sides discussed substantive plans for next steps, which will be announced in the coming weeks, and look forward to equally productive meetings tomorrow in Ukraine."

item.title: Scoop: Republican midterms convention speakers revealed
item.description:
President Trump and his top allies will share the stage with Republican candidates in some of the nation's most competitive races at next week's GOP midterm convention in Dallas, according to a preliminary list of speakers obtained by Axios.

Why it matters: The lineup underscores a central purpose of the convention: firing up Trump voters and getting them to turn out in November, even though the president isn't on the ballot.

Driving the news: Trump will speak both nights of the Sept. 9-10 convention, while Vice President Vance will deliver a keynote address on the second night.

  • The lineup also includes Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt and Donald Trump Jr.
  • House Speaker Mike Johnson, Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso and National Republican Senatorial Committee Chair Tim Scott are among the congressional leaders who will appear.
  • One name that is notably absent from the list is Senate Majority Leader John Thune, who Trump has attacked for not doing more to pass election security legislation. But Thune is scheduled to be in Dallas next week for fundraising, and organizers say they are still adding names to the list.
  • Republicans in some of the toughest races aren't attending, including Sen. Susan Collins in Maine and former Sen. John Sununu in New Hampshire.

Zoom out: Republicans will use the convention to mobilize Trump voters, who party strategists worry will be less inclined to turn out than they were two years ago.

  • Much of the two-day event will be focused on branding Democrats as far-outside-the-mainstream socialists.

Zoom in: The convention will put Trump onstage alongside Republicans running in many of the races that will determine control of Congress.

  • Senate candidates include Ohio Sen. Jon Husted, Texas Republican Ken Paxton, Michigan Republican Mike Rogers, North Carolina Republican Michael Whatley and Georgia Rep. Mike Collins. Trump won all five states in 2024, though all of them are competitive this year.
  • On the House side, New York Rep. Mike Lawler and Pennsylvania Reps. Rob Bresnahan and Ryan Mackenzie are among the vulnerable incumbents slated to speak, along with Wisconsin Rep. Derrick Van Orden.
  • Lawler is the only House candidate on the roster running in a district Kamala Harris carried in 2024.

Yes, but: Appearing at the convention isn't without risk for Republicans in tight races.

  • Democrats are likely to portray them as closely aligned with Trump, whose approval rating was in the 30s in several recent polls.

By the numbers: About 100 Republican lawmakers and candidates are expected to attend the convention, either as speakers or in the audience. A number of non-politicians will also address the convention.

Here is the list of speakers:

Keynote Speakers

  • President Trump, Night One Keynote Address and Night Two Closing Remarks
  • Vice President Vance, Night Two Keynote Address
  • Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent
  • Attorney General Todd Blanche
  • HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
  • Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz
  • HUD Secretary Scott Turner
  • Former press secretary Karoline Leavitt
  • Donald Trump Jr.

Republican Leadership

  • Speaker Mike Johnson
  • Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso
  • Senator Tim Scott, National Republican Senatorial Committee Chairman
  • House Majority Leader Steve Scalise
  • House Majority Whip Tom Emmer
  • House Republican Conference Chair Lisa McClain
  • NRCC Chair Richard Hudson
  • Republican National Committee Chairman Joe Gruters

Elected Officials

  • Sen. Ted Cruz (Texas)
  • Sen. Jon Husted (Ohio)
  • Sen. Dave McCormick (Pa.)
  • Gov. Greg Abbott (Texas)
  • Texas Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick
  • Texas Attorney General and Senate candidate Ken Paxton
  • Rep. Rob Bresnahan (Pa.)
  • Georgia Senate candidate Rep. Mike Collins
  • Rep. Monica De La Cruz (Texas)
  • Florida governor candidate Rep. Byron Donalds
  • Rep. Brandon Gill (Texas)
  • Rep. Brian Jack (Ga.)
  • Rep. Mike Lawler (N.Y.)
  • Rep. Anna Paulina Luna (Fla.)
  • Rep. Ryan Mackenzie (Pa.)
  • Rep. Jason Smith (Mo.)
  • Rep. Derrick Van Orden (Wis.)
  • Dallas Mayor Eric Johnson

Candidates

  • Captain Mike Bouchard Jr., Candidate for U.S. House (MI-10)
  • Laurie Buckhout, Candidate for U.S. House (NC-01)
  • Greg Cunningham, Candidate for U.S. House (NM-02)
  • Jay Feely, Candidate for U.S. House (AZ-01)
  • Eric Flores, Candidate for U.S. House (TX-34)
  • Carlos De La Cruz, Candidate for U.S. House (TX-35)
  • Mike LiPetri, Candidate for U.S. House (NY-03)
  • Derek Merrin, Candidate for U.S. House (OH-09)
  • Marty O'Donnell, Candidate for U.S. House (NV-03)
  • Mike Rogers, Candidate for U.S. Senate (MI)
  • Tano Tijerina, Candidate for U.S. House (TX-28)
  • Michael Whatley, Candidate for U.S. Senate (NC)

item.title: U.S. attacks 3 Iranian tankers in tit-for-tat response
item.description:
U.S. forces struck three Iranian oil tankers Saturday after Iran fired ballistic missiles at two U.S. Navy warships, U.S. Central Command said.

Why it matters: The strikes continue a tit-for-tat war that just passed the six-month mark.

  • A U.S. official told Axios this week it had a new "tanker-for-tanker" policy approved by President Trump.

Driving the news: CENTCOM said it retaliated after a U.S. aircraft carrier and guided-missile destroyer evaded missiles fired by Iran.

  • The U.S. attacks "permanently disabled" the M/T Downy and the M/T Stark 1, CENTCOM said in a news release.
  • They also "completely destroyed" the M/T Kylo in the Gulf of Oman after the crew was warned to abandon ship.
  • CENTCOM posted footage of the strikes on social media.

The big picture: On the first day of the war, Trump told Axios he "can go long and take over the whole thing, or end it in two or three days."

  • The next day, he predicted to the Daily Mail the military campaign would "take four weeks — or less." Six months later, the U.S. and Iran are still trading attacks.
  • The latest exchange came a day after Trump called the Iran conflict "small potatoes" and two days after Vice President Vance insisted there was no war and "no active shooting" between the two.
  • An Aug. 14–17 Economist/YouGov poll found 65% of Americans want the U.S. to make a deal to end the war as quickly as possible.

item.title: "We're stuck:" GOP accepts Trump's all-about-me midterms
item.description:
President Trump is hitting the campaign trail and doing the last thing many Republicans want: making the 59 days to the Nov. 3 midterms a referendum on him.

  • At the same time, they know it's inevitable.

Why it matters: Most Republicans are too scared to bluntly tell Trump how unpopular he is. And Trump wants an unprecedented convention next week, ads and events to focus on him.

The big picture: Their timidity aside, Republicans need Trump's low-propensity voters to turn out. So they're going along with a Trump-focused strategy that many believe could cost them credibility — along with seats in the House and Senate.

  • "We have no choice. We're stuck on the boat with him whether we like it or not," said a top Republican campaign official who's in contact with Trump's political operation.
  • "Now, a rising tide raises all boats," the official added. "But the only ones who sound sure about the tide rising is the White House."

Driving the news: At Trump's urging, the GOP on Wednesday and Thursday is hosting an unprecedented midterm convention in Dallas, headlined by the president.

Zoom in: Trump plans to speak both nights at the convention. He's also the star of his political operation's first two TV ads:

  • The first 30-second ad, called "Toughest Guy," is all about you-know-who.
  • The second, labeled "Tax Cut Prices," features Trump as well and would be more conventional for a campaign in which he's on the ballot.

Inside the room: Trump essentially demanded the ads focus on him because midterms are referendums on a president anyway, and he wanted to tout his accomplishments, The Atlantic first reported.

  • "I'm not on the ballot but I'm on the ballot," Trump told one confidant who relayed the conversation to Axios.
  • "Our job is to turn Trump voters into midterm voters," a Trump adviser told Axios.

The intrigue: The ads look like a de facto compromise between Trump and his political staff.

  • "This is for the audience of one," Trump's confidant said, referring to the president. "If the boss wants it, he gets it."
  • One Trump adviser said to expect more conventional ads: "We will be stripping the bark off of Democrats and supporting our candidates. ... It's not all Trump-focused ads."

What he's saying: On Friday, Trump acknowledged to reporters that "history has said that the sitting president" sees midterm losses, but he didn't complete the thought and then talked about how "nobody's ever had a first one and a half years like we have."

  • "We have around $1 billion that I can spend," Trump said, referring to his super PAC and political nonprofit, which together have about $800 million.
  • "I'm allocating, probably, about $400-$500 million" for the midterms, he said.
  • "This is my money that I control now," he said. "I can spend it for what I want to spend it for. But I'm going to help a lot of the congressmen and senators that need help."

Yes, but: It's unclear how Trump could spend that much money in two months.

Between the lines: Trump's message in his tax cut ads is good, Republican strategists say, but their research increasingly shows voters blame him for the war in Iran that's raising gas prices.

  • "Diesel's at an all-time high. Gas is about $4 a gallon. We can't message that away," said another Republican who runs campaigns for a few federal candidates.
  • Trump advisers say he'll use the bully pulpit to make his case at the convention, but his speeches tend to lack cogency and focus, and their effectiveness is questionable.
  • "If you look at the 20 competitive House races and the six Senate races we're really focused on, this is not as dire as the media wants you to think," a Trump adviser said. "This is winnable."

The backstory: Trump explained this week on the "Lt. Dan" podcast with Texas Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick that he decided to hold the event in Dallas because "we have this big convention for the presidential election, but the midterms — people talk about it. It's very important, but there's no convention."

  • "So ... I just came up with the idea, and we raised a lot of money."

Friction point: Trump's plummeting poll numbers aside, one problem is the convention's timing: It's competing with the NFL's season-opening games, which could draw far more attention.

  • Even Republicans' interest is limited. Many candidates aren't going.
  • "What's the point?" yet another Republican consultant involved in federal races told Axios. "It's like what they say about a tree falling in a forest: Does it make a noise if nobody's around? Well, is it a convention if no one's really watching?"

What's next: At a Rose Garden dinner Wednesday with dozens of House Republicans, Trump promised to campaign across the country in 35 races "to see if we can get everyone elected."

  • If Trump wants to campaign for a candidate, it's going to be hard for them to say no, said one of the consultants involved in talks with MAGA Inc., the super PAC that backs Trump.
  • "Say no to Trump, and he could punish you," the consultant said. "Say yes to him, and his presence might not help. This is the world we're in."

item.title: Republicans sour on the economy
item.description:
Republicans' confidence in the economy has plummeted over the last six months at a pace unseen since Covid — reminiscent of the declines during the global financial crisis nearly two decades ago.

Why it matters: Usually, the president's party is upbeat about the economy, while the party out of power is far more downcast. What's striking now is that Republicans have grown increasingly sour this year, even with a Republican president in office.

  • It's another in a long list of ominous indicators for President Trump heading into the final two months before Election Day.

By the numbers: Since February, Republican consumer sentiment has plunged 15.1 index points, from 97.1 to 82, according to the latest University of Michigan Surveys of Consumers data. Democratic sentiment has fallen just 1.6 index points, from 41.8 to 40.2.

  • The 82 reading is lower than at any point during either of Trump's presidencies, with one exception: December 2020, after he had lost reelection but before he left office.
Data: University of Michigan Surveys of Consumers; Chart: Mike Zapler/Axios

Flashback: It's rare for one party's outlook to remain steady while the other's falls — typically they move in tandem. But a similar split occurred during the global financial crisis in late 2008 and early 2009.

Caveat: That period included the election and inauguration of a Democratic president, accounting for some of the Republican decline.

What they're saying: "The vast majority of the time, Republicans and Democrats move broadly in parallel," Joanne Hsu, director of the Surveys of Consumers, told Axios. But that is not the case now.

  • "Republicans were expecting very positive results from administration policies" on the economy, including tariffs, she added. "But they haven't seen a slowdown in inflation, let alone" the reduction in prices that Trump promised.

Yes, but: Hsu said it's important to remember that, despite the slide, Republicans still have a much more positive outlook on the economy than Democrats.

  • For instance, Republicans still broadly believe gas prices will fall once the Iran war is over, which is not the case with Democrats, she said.

Zoom in: The Michigan survey tracks with other data on how Republicans feel about the economy under Trump, including a July Pew Research poll.

  • Forty-one percent of Republicans or Republican-leaning independents called the economy excellent or good — down 8 percentage points from January.
  • And the share of Republicans who said Trump's policies have made the economy worse rose from 18 percent to 28 percent. The share who said the policies have improved conditions dropped from 57 percent to 42 percent.

The other side: "The hard data of consumer spending and retail sales have, for months, consistently reinforced that the American consumer remains resilient thanks to the President's proven economic agenda of tax cuts and deregulation," said White House spokesman Kush Desai.

  • "As the Administration's economic policies, trade deals, and trillions in investments continue to materialize, Americans can count on more progress to come," he added.

The bottom line: It's no secret that the election will turn on the economy. Inflation remains untamed, and the war in Iran shows no sign of ending.

  • Trump has always been able to rely on bedrock support from Republicans, but even that is starting to crack.

item.title: Trump envoys Witkoff and Kushner to travel to Moscow and Kyiv this weekend
item.description:
President Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will travel this weekend to Moscow and Kyiv for talks on ending the war, U.S. officials said.

Why it matters: This will be the first visit by Witkoff and Kushner to Kyiv since President Trump returned to office.

  • "They're bringing with them a plan to end the war," Trump told reporters in the Oval Office on Friday.

State of play: Witkoff and Kushner will travel on Friday, hold talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin at the Kremlin on Saturday and then meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in Kyiv on Sunday.

  • The visit by Trump's envoys comes 10 days after CIA Director John Ratcliffe met with the heads of the Russian intelligence and security services in Moscow.
  • Ratcliffe was trying to learn whether the Russian intelligence chiefs could persuade Putin to pursue diplomacy with the goal of ending the war.
  • Witkoff and Kushner met with President Trump at the White House Thursday to discuss the trip.

Between the lines: Ukrainian and U.S. officials said they've been discussing the Kyiv trip for months.

  • In recent days, they said, the trip was on and off several times for different reasons before they settled on this weekend.

Catch up quick: Negotiations between Russia and Ukraine mediated by the Trump administration were paused in mid-February after the Iran war started.

  • Witkoff and Kushner have held separate talks over the past few months with Russian and Ukrainian negotiators, but little progress has been made.
  • Zelensky's chief of staff, Kyrylo Budanov, told local media last week that U.S.-mediated talks with Russia could resume in September.

Yes, but: Ukrainian officials are highly skeptical of Putin's intentions and say they have intelligence that suggests Putin is planning a major escalation of the war.

  • Russia has also intensified missile and drone strikes on Ukrainian cities, including Kyiv.
  • Zelensky's deputy chief of staff, Pavlo Palisa, told reporters on Friday that Putin has ordered his military to prepare several operational scenarios for an offensive in northern Ukraine, with Kyiv and Chernihiv identified as key areas.
  • Putin has also rejected several proposals by the Trump administration to hold a trilateral summit with Trump and Zelensky to try to reach a diplomatic breakthrough.

What they're saying: Zelensky confirmed the meetings on X and said Ukraine is preparing for Witkoff and Kushner's visit.

  • He noted that Ukraine agreed not to conduct airstrikes against Russia on Saturday so that the U.S. envoys can arrive safely.
  • "Russia must do the same, ensuring there are no air strikes from its side for the time needed to hold these talks and handle the logistical matters related to this American visit," Zelensky said.
  • He said Ukraine wants the talks with Kushner and Witkoff to be substantive. "We will see what proposals Steve and Jared bring and what they are told in Moscow in response," he said.

item.title: A costly summer sendoff approaches
item.description:
Persistent pump pain and pricey burgers mean this summer's last hurrah comes with a cost crunch.

The big picture: Gasoline prices are almost certain to remain north of $4 per gallon over Labor Day weekend — a heavy travel stretch and the time when midterm election season intensifies.

Driving the news: Labor Day gas prices are slated to be the highest on record, surpassing the previous one set in 2012, per market tracking firm GasBuddy and AAA.

  • That's coming off a record-setting August, where the monthly national average of $4.07 trounced 2022's record, per AAA data.
  • While regular gas prices are more likely to impact Labor Day travel than diesel, the fuel that powers America's trucking fleet hit a new high Friday, driving up costs across a wide swath of industries.
Data: AAA; Chart: Erin Davis/Axios Visuals

Friction point: Meanwhile, the war in Iran is showing signs of intensifying and has scrambled markets.

  • The Wall Street Journal reported this week that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is quietly extending troop deployments, citing people familiar, while the president maintains the U.S. can strike "any time we want."

By the numbers: The number of Americans who say gas prices are going up has nearly doubled in the past six months, per the Ipsos Consumer Tracker.

  • In March, just 38% of people thought prices were higher. Now, that's up to 79%.
  • Ipsos' Matt Carmichael writes that in "a question we've asked about 20 times in recent years, we've never seen such a sudden and dramatic shift."

For travelers flying to top Labor Day destinations, airfare is nearly 20% higher than last year, per AAA.

  • Still, TSA predicts over 17 million travelers at airports across the country between the Thursday and Wednesday that straddle Labor Day.
  • About 2.87 million travelers are expected to take off the Friday before Labor Day. Last year, the TSA recorded its highest volume ever for the Friday before Labor Day with some 2.97 million passengers.

Yes, but: Once travelers touch down — or even among those opting for a staycation and grilling at home — beef prices for those Labor Day burgers remain stubbornly elevated.

  • A pound of ground beef cost $6.89 on average in July, up 10% from the year prior.

The bottom line: This Labor Day might hurt pocketbooks more than usual — and the market is feeling it too, as higher energy prices show up across the economy.

  • And as affordability looms over the midterms, more than a month of averages over $4 per gallon and persistently high beef costs could give the GOP holiday heartburn.

Go deeper: Gas prices are rising again — and so is GOP grief in the midterms

item.title: Scoop: Trump administration drafting post-war Middle East plan
item.description:
The Trump administration is working on a post-war strategy focused on a regional effort to contain Iran and expand normalization of relations between Israel and its neighbors, according to two U.S. officials and two other sources with knowledge of the issue.

Why it matters: While the plan is still in the early stages of drafting, it's intended to guide the U.S. approach in the Middle East after the Iran war ends and in the final two years of President Trump's term. Two big events loom over the planning: the Oct. 27 election in Israel and the U.S. midterm elections in November.

Behind the scenes: The initial work on the strategy is taking place both at the senior political level of the Trump administration and at the working level across agencies, U.S. officials say.

  • In recent weeks, Trump has held two meetings with senior advisers where the plan was discussed and ideas were raised, sources say.
  • Trump has said in private conversations that he's working on "something much bigger" in the Middle East after the war with Iran.
  • The White House declined to comment.

Three main elements have been raised as possible parts of the strategy, according to the sources:

  • Creating a regional alignment among U.S. allies to contain Iran, with the U.S. as a guarantor. 
  • Making a concerted effort to bring the regional fallout from the Oct. 7, 2023, attacks closer to a conclusion by securing the next phase of Trump's Gaza plan, reaching a security agreement between Israel and Syria, and implementing the Israel-Lebanon agreement.
  • Expanding the Abraham Accords and reaching a Saudi-Israeli normalization agreement.  

The intrigue: The Trump administration hopes that any new Israeli government formed after the Oct. 27 election will be willing and able to cooperate in the post-war strategy.

  • But some U.S. officials stress that Trump will push to implement it regardless of the Israeli election results — and even if they produce a political stalemate.

What to watch: A source briefed on the process said it will take another few weeks to draft the strategy. "They are cooking it, but it is not yet cooked," the source said.

  • "The idea is to tie a whole lot of things in the region together — how you create a regional alignment after the war. It is still unclear if all U.S. allies in the region will be on board," the person added.

item.title: Maria Bartiromo fired by Fox
item.description:
Fox News Media fired longtime host Maria Bartiromo for business reasons, a spokesperson confirmed to Axios on Thursday.

Why it matters: Bartiromo is considered one of the network's most high profile hosts.

  • The unexpected departure prompted questions about whether she would join the Trump administration.
  • Bartiromo has developed a strong rapport with the president over the last decade.
  • The White House didn't immediately respond to requests for comment.

What they're saying: In a statement, Fox News Media said, "We thank Maria for her work over the last 12 ½ years and wish her all the best on her next chapter."

  • Bartiromo was last on air Aug. 9.

The other side: Bartiromo's attorney Bryan Freedman called reports that she was fired or no longer a Fox employee "unequivocally false."

  • "Make no mistake, we have the receipts and witnesses and they will come out whether through the courthouse or otherwise," he said in a statement.

President Trump noted Bartiromo's ouster in a post to Truth Social late Thursday night.

  • "Maria is a total professional, and a true warrior. Her fans, of which there are many, will not be happy. God bless you, Maria!" he wrote.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with comments by President Trump and Maria Bartiromo's attorney.

  • The White House didn't immediately respond to requests for comment.

What they're saying: In a statement, Fox News Media said, "We thank Maria for her work over the last 12 ½ years and wish her all the best on her next chapter."

  • Bartiromo was last on air Aug. 9.

The other side: Bartiromo's attorney Bryan Freedman called reports that she was fired or no longer a Fox employee "unequivocally false."

  • "Make no mistake, we have the receipts and witnesses and they will come out whether through the courthouse or otherwise," he said in a statement.

President Trump noted Bartiromo's ouster in a post to Truth Social late Thursday night.

  • "Maria is a total professional, and a true warrior. Her fans, of which there are many, will not be happy. God bless you, Maria!" he wrote.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with comments by President Trump and Maria Bartiromo's attorney.

item.title: Scoop: Rep. Analilia Mejia launches super PAC to fund more progressive upsets
item.description:
After winning an upset primary victory over a field of better-funded, establishment-backed rivals, Rep. Analilia Mejia (D-N.J.) is launching a super PAC to help other progressive underdogs do the same, Axios has learned.

Why it matters: Mejia is adding to a growing constellation of new progressive super PACs trying to compete with cash-rich groups like AIPAC that back more moderate Democrats in primaries.

  • It is all part of a strategy that has helped the left pull off a series of high-profile primary victories this election cycle over incumbents and establishment favorites.
  • "We're ready to build a new class of unbought, unbossed candidates who will refuse corporate PAC money, and will stand for the values that the American people are demanding," Mejia said in a statement.

Driving the news: Mejia's group, "Unbought, Unbossed PAC," will train and fund "working-class and underrepresented community leaders" running for office, according to a press release first shared with Axios.

  • It will also provide "voter education resources and voter protection training" and build "a nationwide community of candidates, organizers, and local leaders who can learn from one another and organize beyond any single election."
  • "Unbought, Unbossed PAC is about finding the next generation of leaders who are already fighting for their communities and giving them the tools to run, organize, and win," Mejia said.

Catch up quick: Mejia defeated nearly a dozen Democratic primary rivals in a February special election to replace New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill in Congress.

  • The former progressive organizer was outraised by five of her primary rivals, bringing in just $420,000 to the $1.2 million raised by former Rep. Tom Malinowski, who finished second.
  • Mejia's victory was widely considered an upset and was inadvertently spurred, at least in part, by AIPAC spending $2.3 million against Malinowski.

What to watch: The super PAC will only support candidates who refuse to take corporate PAC money and who support banning members of Congress from trading stocks, according to the press release.

  • "It's time we start uplifting your nontraditional candidates who aren't lawyers or billionaires, but everyday Americans," Mejia said.
  • She added: "A Congress that looks and feels like America will better serve this nation."

item.title: America's jobs scare recedes
item.description:
The labor market looks considerably healthier than it did at the start of the summer.

Why it matters: Friday morning's jobs report recast the last two months as a period of modest job growth rather than of outright deterioration, capped by a gain last month that was more than triple what economists expected.

  • The labor market is weathering the Iran conflict and an AI-driven transformation of the economy with surprisingly little damage, at least for now.
  • For the Federal Reserve, the report puts inflation even more squarely in focus — with less evidence that the labor market is too fragile to hold up in the event of higher interest rates.

What they're saying: "August turned the heat back up on the job market," Glassdoor chief economist Daniel Zhao wrote Friday morning.

  • But Zhao noted that "the data has swung hard from month to month, and revisions keep rewriting what we thought we knew, so the underlying trend is tough to read."
Data: Bureau of Labor Statistics; Chart: Courtenay Brown/Axios

Driving the news: Employers added a surprisingly strong 162,000 jobs in August, the biggest gain since March. The unemployment rate was unchanged at 4.1%.

  • Paired with positive revisions to June and July numbers, the release lifts three-month average job gains to 71,000, from just 20,000.
  • June and July payrolls were revised up by a combined 55,000, a revision that flipped July from a 23,000-job loss to a 21,000-job gain.

Between the lines: What looked like a labor market shedding jobs this summer now looks like one that slowed but kept expanding.

  • August's headline was boosted by 42,000 jobs added in local government education, which largely reversed July's decline.
  • That suggests some of the summer's apparent weakness — and August's subsequent rebound — reflected seasonal volatility rather than a sudden shift in labor demand.

Zoom in: Bars and restaurants added 59,000 jobs in August, a surprising result considering that the World Cup ended in July and that it seemed plausible there would be a falloff in the sector's employment.

  • Manufacturing added another 16,000 jobs, continuing an upward trend in employment that started late last year.
  • The jobs contraction in the information sector — which includes tech infrastructure, publishing and media jobs — deepened, shedding 23,000 jobs in August and 115,000 over the past year.

By the numbers: The unemployment rate held at 4.1% (though the unrounded rate edged up to 4.14% from 4.09%). The details of the household survey were promising.

  • The labor force participation rate rebounded to 61.6%, reversing some of a steep two-month slide in which nearly 1 million people had exited the workforce. Still, participation remains 0.7 point below a year ago.
  • The share of prime-age Americans — those aged between 25 and 54 — with a job held at 80.4% in August, still below its recent high of 80.8% in May.

What to watch: August may help clarify whether the recent hiring slowdown reflected fewer workers available or less appetite among employers to hire.

  • About 700,000 people entered the labor force last month and most found work, suggesting that employers were able to absorb a sudden influx of workers.
  • That follows a stretch when a shrinking labor force kept unemployment low, obscuring whether weak hiring reflected limited worker supply or weak labor demand.

The risk of a sharp labor market downturn looks considerably smaller than it did a month ago.

  • Still unresolved is whether hiring is accelerating again or simply settling into a slower — though still solid — equilibrium.

The solid numbers add ammunition for those Fed officials who see an urgent need to raise interest rates to bring inflation down.

The big picture: With the labor market hovering at something near full employment but inflation in its sixth year of exceeding the Fed's 2% target, the decision of whether to raise interest rates in less than two weeks comes down to two key August inflation indicators due out next week.

  • The best that can be said of the robust jobs report is that it affirms the preexisting view of the central bank's leaders that the big question now is around inflation.
  • Nothing in the report would act as a caution flag for those who might seek a rate hike, and indeed the data supports the idea that the job market could even be reaccelerating.
  • "August payrolls were strong across the board, including in cyclical sectors like construction and manufacturing," Sonu Varghese, global macro strategist at Carson Group, wrote in a note. "Add in elevated inflation, and the Fed looks well offsides against an economy that's running hot."

Yes, but: The jobs report has often been the most important monthly economic data release for parsing what the Fed will do next. Not now.

  • The August numbers don't so much turn the overall economic narrative as affirm chairman Kevin Warsh's statement in a speech last week that "I believe the labor markets are consistent with full employment."

What's next: Next week's releases of the August Producer Price Index on Thursday and the Consumer Price Index on Friday have now taken on greater importance for interest rate decisions.

  • Economists can, by combining elements of the two, come up with a quite accurate estimate of where the Fed's preferred inflation measure, the Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index, will land when it is released Sept. 30.

The bottom line: The jobs numbers bolstered the case for a rate hike, but next week's inflation numbers are more likely to settle the decision one way or the other.

item.title: The coming verdict on Trump's Strait of Hormuz claims
item.description:
The White House is at odds with some private sector analysts over how much oil is leaving the Strait of Hormuz — but it will take weeks until the picture of what's truly getting through becomes clear.

Why it matters: How much oil exits the waterway sways the price of gasoline and other consumer products.

  • The White House is claiming success in forcing open the world's most important energy chokepoint, which handled 20 million barrels of crude and oil products each day before the Iran war.
  • The verdict could arrive as fall election campaigns near fever pitch.

Driving the news: President Trump claimed yesterday that 18 million barrels per day are moving, saying via Truth Social that "Hormuz Volumes are BACK."

  • Energy Secretary Chris Wright told CNBC Tuesday that 17 million barrels of crude and products combined flowed on Monday, but he has also noted the multi-day rolling average is much lower.

What we're watching: There's not enough information to know precisely now — but more data will emerge that will better reveal how much oil movements have recently risen.

  • "We will know the truth or closer to it in a few weeks. If all that oil came out, it has to go somewhere and eventually it will be recorded," Rapidan Energy Group founder and president Bob McNally said via email.

The intrigue: Tanker tracking services have tallied less oil than some of the administration's claims in recent weeks.

  • But barrel counting is a mix of art and science, especially in wartime. Many tankers are going dark by turning off their "automatic identification system" transponders and using other tactics to move oil.
  • That makes things harder for market intelligence firms, though they rely on multiple information sources like satellite imagery and cargo loading data.
  • Port and customs information in oil-buying countries, and the size of their crude stockpiles, will complement the outbound data estimates. But it takes tankers weeks to reach some major importers.

What they're saying: "In coordination with the U.S. military, the U.S. Department of Energy maintains the best available data related to oil and oil products leaving the Arabian gulf," an Energy Department spokesperson said via email.

Between the lines: The 17 million barrels that Wright claimed may be plausible on a given day, analysts say, though what's most important is the multi-day average.

  • Wright said early this week that flows have been averaging around 8 million barrels per day, per Bloomberg.
  • The Energy Department spokesperson told Axios that on Wednesday, nearly 12 million barrels of oil and oil products moved through the strait.

My thought bubble: While analysts are skeptical of some of the eye-popping administration claims, there's rough agreement between some private sector trackers and the Energy Department's multi-day average tally.

State of play: Apples-to-apples comparisons are tricky, depending on the time period and what's getting counted.

  • Data from Vortexa, a commodity tracking and intelligence firm, shows a 28-day moving average of around 8 million barrels of crude and products as of August 31, per senior analyst Rohit Rathod.
  • Tanker Trackers, another firm, said Wednesday that its preliminary data shows crude transit specifically rising to an average of 5.94 million barrels per day over the past seven days.

The bottom line: Eurasia Group analyst Gregory Brew says it appears more oil is indeed making it out. "It's probably not as much as they are claiming," he said of the Trump administration.

  • "But it's enough to give Trump the idea that time is on his side, and that the US has the upper hand over the Iranians," Brew said via email.

Sign up here for Axios' Future of Energy newsletter.

item.title: AI models are becoming unknowable
item.description:
AI models may be getting safer while also getting harder to monitor. Which side of that seesaw prevails could determine whether AI is scaled safely or ruins civilization as we know it.

Why it matters: Right now both options are running full steam and no one knows who's in charge of making sure the right one wins.

State of play: OpenAI on Thursday released GPT-6 Astra, which president Greg Brockman said could eventually be seen as the start of artificial general intelligence, or AGI.

  • Astra performs better, but it's also better at avoiding monitoring, meaning it could be harder to know what it's thinking or doing.
  • OpenAI CEO Sam Altman separately told Axios this week that models are becoming "superhuman" in some capabilities and that "we are just sailing in unknown waters."

Between the lines: The top leaders of AI companies are sounding the alarm on their own technology just as it gets harder to understand a model's actions.

  • OpenAI, Anthropic and more than 100 other companies warned that time is running out to prepare for AI-enabled attacks on critical infrastructure.
  • Altman told Axios that Congress is struggling to figure out how to regulate such a fast moving technology.
  • "We've been talking to some external organizations about potential concrete standards we could put in place" OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki told reporters, adding that OpenAI has also been working to strengthen its own processes.

Threat level: While awaiting regulation, AI models are becoming unknowable.

  • OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki said on a call with reporters that it would continue to get harder to monitor the thoughts of AI models over time.
  • The Information reported this week that the latest OpenAI model used a new technique to boost its performance that may have also made its thoughts less transparent (OpenAI disputes that reporting.)
  • In an analysis of a cyber incident in which an OpenAI model broke into the Hugging Face AI library to get the answers to a benchmark test, one researcher said AI agents generate so much activity that humans can't realistically monitor them without the use of more AI.

What they're saying: "This is an even bigger deal than Hugging Face," Sydney Von Arx, an AI Safety researcher and founder of the nonprofit Nightingale told Axios regarding lack of insight into model reasoning.

  • The concern is that, over time, a model's thinking could happen in a hidden layer, which means it could do bad stuff without us knowing.
  • OpenAI says this is not the case with Astra: the model doesn't write out its reasoning as often as prior models do, but that was not done intentionally.
  • Regardless, if models do less thinking out loud some researchers worry their behavior will be harder to monitor.

The bottom line: AI is getting sneakier and even the executives driving its growth are asking for help monitoring the risks.

item.title: EU tech chief: AI guardrails inevitable for U.S.
item.description:
CHAPEL HILL, N.C. — The Trump administration used this week's G20 innovation summit to draw a bright line between U.S. and European approaches to AI regulation. The bloc's top tech official says the U.S. is ending up with many of the same guardrails anyway.

Why it matters: The U.S. is urging countries to avoid Europe's sweeping approach to AI regulation, but the fight is shifting to which guardrails advanced AI needs and how governments put them in place.

What they're saying: European Commission tech chief Henna Virkkunen told Axios that the two sides often end up addressing the same safety concerns, even if U.S. safeguards are starting to emerge through state laws and court cases rather than something broad like the EU AI Act.

  • "We see when it comes to technologies that in the USA the culture is different. So often it's coming via court cases, but often very similar things anyway, very similar concerns."
  • "I don't see that this is so like black and white," Virkkunen said.
  • ChatGPT is officially facing strict rules under the Digital Services Act, for instance, and Virkkunen said it's important for the EU to simplify the bloc's rules and make the region "easier, simpler, faster" for businesses.

The big picture: The U.S. hasn't adopted sweeping federal AI rules, but Washington is still shaping how companies develop and deploy advanced models through executive actions, voluntary frameworks, national security restrictions and other policy.

  • Meanwhile, states are moving ahead with varying degrees of AI regulation, and product changes are being forced on companies through lawsuits.

Zoom in: The EU is working on a framework for pre-deployment testing and trusted partner access, Virkkunen noted, another area where the EU is working through similar AI policy questions facing the U.S.

  • "So in [the] European Union, we are also working for that blueprint, and we are continuing to discuss also under G7, especially with our partners, how we should work on this topic."
  • The Trump administration has developed a voluntary framework for reviewing some advanced AI models before release, including potentially giving government officials access for up to 30 days. The White House does not plan to publicly release this framework.
  • OpenAI's Sam Altman confirmed this week to Axios that the administration reviewed its Astra model and noted the process is voluntary: "But we of course did it."

Industry leaders at the G20 innovation summit knocked the EU approach to regulation in remarks before Virkkunen as well as representatives from Germany, France and Italy.

  • In response to White House Office of Science and Technology Policy Director Michael Kratsios' question about what foreign governments should and should not do, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said an approach that's "relatively free of regulation" is the way to go.
  • It's "pretty straightforward," Musk said. "You have to have an environment that's relatively free of regulation, meaning that new things must be default legal as opposed to default illegal."
  • "In the EU, for example, we find that the regulation level is extraordinarily high, and things are generally default illegal, and this inhibits progress with new technologies. It slows it down."

The bottom line: As AI has grown more powerful, Washington has increasingly gotten involved with model releases.

The big picture: The U.S. hasn't adopted sweeping federal AI rules, but Washington is still shaping how companies develop and deploy advanced models through executive actions, voluntary frameworks, national security restrictions and other policy.

  • Meanwhile, states are moving ahead with varying degrees of AI regulation, and product changes are being forced on companies through lawsuits.

Zoom in: The EU is working on a framework for pre-deployment testing and trusted partner access, Virkkunen noted, another area where the EU is working through similar AI policy questions facing the U.S.

  • "So in [the] European Union, we are also working for that blueprint, and we are continuing to discuss also under G7, especially with our partners, how we should work on this topic."
  • The Trump administration has developed a voluntary framework for reviewing some advanced AI models before release, including potentially giving government officials access for up to 30 days. The White House does not plan to publicly release this framework.
  • OpenAI's Sam Altman confirmed this week to Axios that the administration reviewed its Astra model and noted the process is voluntary: "But we of course did it."

Industry leaders at the G20 innovation summit knocked the EU approach to regulation in remarks before Virkkunen as well as representatives from Germany, France and Italy.

  • In response to White House Office of Science and Technology Policy Director Michael Kratsios' question about what foreign governments should and should not do, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said an approach that's "relatively free of regulation" is the way to go.
  • It's "pretty straightforward," Musk said. "You have to have an environment that's relatively free of regulation, meaning that new things must be default legal as opposed to default illegal."
  • "In the EU, for example, we find that the regulation level is extraordinarily high, and things are generally default illegal, and this inhibits progress with new technologies. It slows it down."

The bottom line: As AI has grown more powerful, Washington has increasingly gotten involved with model releases.

item.title: Diesel price surges to all-time high, fueled by wars
item.description:
The average price of diesel topped its 2022 record high on Friday, spiking to $5.85 per gallon, per AAA.

Why it matters: Farmers, truckers and freight companies have been absorbing higher diesel costs since the Iran war began. The ballooning price threatens to further raise shipping costs while compounding a growing political problem for President Trump.

  • It can also indirectly affect households by putting inflationary pressure on anything Americans buy that's carried by truck, which includes a massive share of goods.

Driving the news: Diesel has been rising steadily for weeks, but surged 17 cents in just the last two days.

  • The previous record was $5.816, per AAA, set in June 2022.
  • Diesel typically costs more than gasoline because of higher taxes, stricter environmental regulations requiring expensive refining and a lower production yield per barrel of oil.

Worth noting: While the strangling of the Strait of Hormuz cast the global market into disarray, Ukraine's highly effective drone campaign targeting Russian refineries has further strained worldwide diesel refinery capacity.

  • "Until that refining supply picture improves, both gasoline and diesel prices face continued upward pressure," Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, writes.
  • The diesel crack spread — the price difference between a barrel of crude and the refined product — hit unprecedented triple-digit highs in recent weeks.

The big picture: "Diesel is an input to virtually everything we consume," says Erich Muehlegger, an economics professor at the University of California-Davis.

  • Diesel price spikes raise production costs in diesel-dependent industries like fishing, farming and construction. For farmers, it's a double whammy, with the war also driving fertilizer costs higher.
  • The record high price comes as the energy-thirsty peak of harvest season looms for corn and soybeans, the nation's largest farm commodities, Axios' Ben Geman reports.

Zoom out: Diesel also fuels the country's trucking fleets. While large carriers like FedEx and UPS have increased their fuel surcharge rates to account for the spiking prices, smaller businesses are more sensitive to volatility.

  • George O'Connor, public affairs director at the Owner-Operator Independent Drivers Association, said in an email to Axios that small business truckers "are the first to feel it when prices jump."
  • Unlike larger competitors, he explained in an email, they can't just raise rates when fuel spikes. Independent truckers, on the other hand, often have less negotiating leverage and work load to load.
  • "With freight rates already low, a sharp increase in diesel can quickly eat up what little margin a small trucking business has left," he added.

This time of year, the U.S. would usually see significant increases in diesel inventory ahead of the fall refinery maintenance season, Jason Miller, a professor in supply chain management at Michigan State University, told Axios.

  • "We could be looking at some basically unprecedented low diesel inventories for that time of the year when we start getting into refinery maintenance season."
  • "Lord forbid we have a catastrophic hurricane," Miller said.

Reality check: Fuel costs are just a fraction of overall prices consumers see, Muehlegger notes.

  • "But the punchline here is that with higher diesel prices, that's putting upward pressure on prices, and upward pressure ... generally within the economy," he says.
  • Miller previously told Axios that gas prices matter more than diesel for the consumer's pocketbook. But for the overall economy, he says, "diesel matters more."

What we're watching: If those price hikes show up in core goods down the line, rather than just retail gasoline or electricity prices, that could make it harder for the Federal Reserve to justify cutting interest rates or even push rates higher.

  • "The Fed is in a box here," John Kilduff, Founding Partner of Again Capital, said recently on CNBC. "They are going to be staring down an inflation pulse now from this renewed price spike."

Go deeper: Here's how to understand crude oil costs and what they mean for gas prices

item.title: U.S. military reviewing deadly strike on Iranian wedding
item.description:
U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) is conducting an internal review of a civilian casualty incident at a wedding during the strikes in Iran on Tuesday, U.S. officials say.

Why it matters: While it still hasn't been confirmed that the incident was caused by the U.S. strike, it is one of the more significant civilian casualty incidents since the war began six months ago.

  • The most significant civilian casualty incident happened on the first day of the war when a U.S. strike hit a school, killing 150 people, most of them children.
  • The U.S. military investigation into that incident is expected to be finalized soon, according to a U.S. official.

Driving the news: According to the Iranian Red Crescent, a humanitarian network, five people were killed and 67 wounded in the blast that hit the home where the wedding was happening.

  • Iranian officials accused the U.S. of striking the building and killing civilians.
  • On Wednesday, CENTCOM commander Admiral Brad Cooper ordered an internal review of the strike, U.S. officials said.
  • "We're aware of the reports, which originated from Iranian state media, and we are looking into them. The U.S. military never targets civilians, unlike the IRGC," CENTCOM spokesman Capt. Tim Hawkins said.

What they're saying: "We're investigating it because obviously we care," Vice President JD Vance said Thursday during a White House press briefing. "We want to know, and if we do make mistakes, again, this is a big difference between us and Iran. When our military makes mistakes, they learn from them to try to get better from them. So we're investigating it very fully."

Behind the scenes: U.S. officials said the strike in the area targeted a communication tower used for both civilian and military communications.

  • As part of the preliminary investigation, CENTCOM is reviewing footage from drones that monitored the area during the strike and the procedures used to identify the target, U.S. officials said.
  • A U.S. official said that in addition to checking whether munitions fired by the U.S. hit the wedding, the investigation will also look at the possibility that an errant Iranian munition fell near the home.
