item.title: House Democrat says his phone calls with a state legislator were wiretapped by FBI
item.description:
Rep. Suhas Subramanyam (D-Va.) said Thursday he was informed by the Department of Justice that his phone calls with a Virginia state legislator in the spring were wiretapped.

Why it matters: The Democratic congressman is casting the tap as part of a pattern of the DOJ targeting President Trump's political enemies, calling the incident "deeply concerning."

  • "They have politically investigated multiple states' Attorneys General and the former FBI director. Now they admit they have surveilled conversations by a sitting Democratic Congressman," Subramanyam said in a statement.
  • The Justice Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Driving the news: Subramanyam released what he said was a notice from the DOJ and the FBI that a federal judge authorized a wiretap in early March that intercepted some of his calls between March 6 and April 5.

  • Subramanyam said the wiretap was part of the DOJ's corruption probe into Louise Lucas, the president pro tempore of the Virginia state Senate, who has denied wrongdoing.
  • Lucas' office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

What they're saying: "The timing of this wiretap and investigation is extremely suspicious," Subramanyam alleged in his statement.

  • "The tap took place between March and May, which was at the peak of campaigning for the redistricting referendum in Virginia. This was also while the Oversight Committee was calling on Pam Bondi to testify on the Epstein investigation."
  • Subramanyam told Axios in a text message he wants to "know how they were using the information," adding, "Were they keeping tabs on me in any way because I'm on Oversight?"

item.title: OpenAI unveils plan to protect critical services from AI cyberattacks
item.description:
OpenAI is launching a new initiative designed to provide subsidized access to its models to water systems, electricity providers, local governments and other critical services.

Why it matters: Critical infrastructure organizations — which have long lacked the budget, manpower and time needed to shore up their cyber defenses — have been struggling to prepare for the anticipated wave of AI-enabled cyberattacks.

Driving the news: OpenAI president Greg Brockman announced the new program while hosting 300 security leaders for a summit at the company's headquarters Thursday.

  • Axios first reported on the summit and Brockman's anticipated announcement.

Zoom in: OpenAI is committing $1 billion to a new Daybreak for Frontline Defenders initiative focused on protecting essential services around the world.

  • The $1 billion will come in the form of expanded subsidized access to models, training, technical support and partnerships for participating organizations.
  • OpenAI is also launching Daybreak for America program, which will provide access to its models to local governments, water systems, electricity providers, regional banks and other critical infrastructure.
  • As part of Daybreak for America, OpenAI is starting a pilot program with the Multi-State Information Sharing and Analysis Center to train cyber defenders at state and local governments on using their models.
  • OpenAI is also working with more than 35 technology and cybersecurity services to embed the AI lab's advanced models into their tools, services and workflows.

Threat level: For years, cyber officials have feared that AI models will soon be capable of autonomously discovering and chaining together vulnerabilities in complex systems that power public utilities and services.

  • While frontier labs like OpenAI have largely restricted access to the advanced cyber capabilities of their most powerful models, rapid improvements in open-weight models' capabilities are raising fears that AI-enabled attacks will be here sooner than anticipated.
  • OpenAI says the new program will allow lesser-resourced utilities to review legacy code, analyze suspicious activity, identify and validate vulnerabilities, prioritize the most serious risks and develop and test security patches.

Reality check: Expanding services and training doesn't solve all of the security problems that have plagued critical infrastructure for decades — which AI-enabled tools will likely now exacerbate.

  • Many entities also need more workers who understand the nuances of protecting the physical systems they're trying to defend from digital threats.

Go deeper: AI is supercharging hacks of everyday utilities

item.title: "Welcome to the AGI era," OpenAI says as GPT-6 Astra debuts
item.description:
OpenAI on Thursday released GPT-6 Astra, which president Greg Brockman called a "generational leap" and said could eventually be seen as the arrival of artificial general intelligence, or AGI.

Why it matters: Astra pushes AI agents closer to doing complex professional work on their own — while also raising questions about how safely they can be deployed.

Driving the news: Brockman says he personally believes OpenAI has reached AGI, while leaving users to decide whether Astra meets that definition.

  • "I think it might be about this model," Brockman said in a briefing with reporters about whether Astra could mark the arrival of AGI.
  • He ended the briefing by saying: "Welcome to the AGI era."

Between the lines: OpenAI said that Astra was built on its largest-ever training run, using more than 100,000 GPUs at its Stargate site in Texas.

  • The company also said this is its first model to use other models in a significant role in supervising Astra's training.
  • GPT-6 Astra will first be available to a limited set of organizations in OpenAI's Daybreak Access program and will be available "in the coming days" for ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business and Enterprise customers and API developers.

Catch-up quick: OpenAI said earlier this week that Astra would be released soon, but that its most powerful cybersecurity capabilities would remain limited to a small group of trusted testers.

  • Astra is the first model OpenAI has designated as reaching its "critical" cybersecurity threshold under its preparedness framework — meaning it can potentially find and exploit previously unknown vulnerabilities across well-protected systems without step-by-step human guidance.
  • OpenAI previously slowed Astra's release to add safety testing after determining that its cyber capabilities could reach the critical threshold.

Zoom in: Astra is designed to work directly inside software, rather than just recommending what a person should do next.

  • In a video demonstration, Astra formatted a legal contract and built a 3D game while handling other tasks, including searching for food and booking a tennis court.
  • OpenAI says Astra can lay out a printed circuit board in KiCad, build a 3D city scene in Unity, create an animated automobile transmission in FreeCAD and Blender, and fill out a tax-return draft from a W-2.
  • In scientific work, the model helped improve a mathematical result on gaps between prime numbers and set new marks on several biology, chemistry, medical and physics evaluations.

Reality check: It remains to be seen just how well Astra can take on these highly advanced tasks in the real world without making critical errors or raising fresh safety concerns.

State of play: it's been a big week for launches with Anthropic, Meta and Google also announcing updates to their leading models.

  • It's also been a time of considerable concern over whether the pace of AI development is faster than society can adjust to the new threats and capabilities.
  • Those worries have grown louder since the July disclosure that OpenAI models in testing escaped from a sandbox and breached the systems of Hugging Face.
  • "When models can do more things autonomously, we have to be able to trust them more," OpenAI research VP Amelia Glaese told reporters. "That's why we took a lot of care, in particular, to teach Astra to stay in bounds of what the user intended."

The intrigue: Much discussion in recent days has centered around whether OpenAI trained Astra in ways that could make it and future models harder for humans to monitor.

  • OpenAI acknowledged that Astra was harder to monitor in evaluations designed to test whether it could evade oversight.
  • The company said the model still appears to struggle to conceal the reasoning needed for complex tasks, but called the decline in monitorability serious and said improving it remains a research priority.
  • "We will need to strengthen our ability to to monitor these models either via extending chain-of-thought monitoring, integrating other ideas like activation monitoring, or finding more specific ways to get the models to be more verbose in their chain of thought," OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki told reporters.

This story is developing.

item.title: A record 47% want stronger unions. Labor's challenge is turning support into power.
item.description:
For only the second time in a quarter century, a majority of Republicans — 52% — approve of labor unions, according to a new Gallup poll.

Why it matters: Despite Americans' rising approval, union membership remains near a modern low. Congress has repeatedly blocked labor's biggest priorities, and House Republicans are now investigating unions, even as their own voters approve of them.

  • Republicans' warmer feelings toward unions don't translate into wanting them to wield more power: 49% of Republicans want unions to have less influence, compared with just 19% who want them to have more.
Data: Gallup Poll Social Series; Chart: Andrew Pantazi/Axios

By the numbers: Overall, 71% of Americans approved of unions, tying the 2022 level. Gallup last recorded higher approval in 1959 at 73%.

  • Approval stands at 89% among Democrats, 70% among independents and 52% among Republicans. The only other time since 2001 that Gallup found majority Republican approval was in 2022.
  • A record 47% of Americans want unions to have more influence, more than double the 23% who want less influence. Another 26% want their influence to remain the same.

The big picture: The latest numbers mark a reversal from the Great Recession. In 2009, union approval bottomed out at 48%, and 42% of Americans wanted unions to have less influence while just 25% wanted them to have more.

Reality check: Americans are embracing unions at a time when few workers belong to one. Just 11% of U.S. workers — 16.5 million — were represented by unions in 2025, compared with 23% and 20.5 million workers in 1983, the first year of comparable data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

  • The most recent year included union representation for less than 7% of private-sector workers.

State of play: Workers have been trying to make up for lost time. Union election petitions filed with the National Labor Relations Board more than doubled from 2021 to 3,286 in 2024. The agency received 2,633 election petitions last year, down from the prior year's peak but still well above earlier years.

  • Americans are skeptical that today's goodwill will translate into greater strength. Just 27% expect unions to become stronger, while 39% expect them to weaken and 29% expect little change, according to the Gallup polling.
Data: Gallup Poll Social Series; Chart: Andrew Pantazi/Axios

Zoom in: Organized labor has repeatedly failed to turn Democratic control of Washington into its biggest legislative prize: rewriting federal law to make it easier for workers to join unions and to win contracts.

  • The Employee Free Choice Act, a signature priority at the start of the Obama administration, would have made it easier for workers to unionize when a majority of workers signed cards. Despite overwhelming Democratic majorities in the House and Senate, it never became law.
  • In 2021, the House passed the Protecting the Right to Organize Act, the next sweeping attempt to rewrite federal labor law, with five Republicans joining Democrats.
  • But it stalled in the Senate where Republicans and even Democratic Sens. Mark Kelly, Mark Warner and Kyrsten Sinema withheld their support.

Between the lines: President Biden leaned on executive action and appointments, creating a task force to promote organizing and pushing the NLRB to favor unionizing workers. In 2023, he became the first president to join striking workers on a picket line, standing with autoworkers in Michigan.

  • The environment has swung sharply. President Trump has used executive orders to remove collective bargaining rights for broad swaths of the federal workforce and to fire the labor board's pro-union general counsel and a Democratic board member.

The latest: House Republicans have also intensified scrutiny of union leadership, launching investigations into the United Auto Workers, United Steelworkers, the American Federation of Teachers and three railroad unions, demanding records about political activity.

The bottom line: Labor has won back popularity it lost during decades of decline, but its harder fight is turning that goodwill into bargaining power and growing its membership.

The fine print: Gallup surveyed 1,200 U.S. adults by cellphone and landline Aug. 3–24. The overall margin of error is 4 percentage points.
item.content:encoded:
For only the second time in a quarter century, a majority of Republicans — 52% — approve of labor unions, according to a new Gallup poll.

Why it matters: Despite Americans' rising approval, union membership remains near a modern low. Congress has repeatedly blocked labor's biggest priorities, and House Republicans are now investigating unions, even as their own voters approve of them.

  • Republicans' warmer feelings toward unions don't translate into wanting them to wield more power: 49% of Republicans want unions to have less influence, compared with just 19% who want them to have more.
Data: Gallup Poll Social Series; Chart: Andrew Pantazi/Axios

By the numbers: Overall, 71% of Americans approved of unions, tying the 2022 level. Gallup last recorded higher approval in 1959 at 73%.

  • Approval stands at 89% among Democrats, 70% among independents and 52% among Republicans. The only other time since 2001 that Gallup found majority Republican approval was in 2022.
  • A record 47% of Americans want unions to have more influence, more than double the 23% who want less influence. Another 26% want their influence to remain the same.

The big picture: The latest numbers mark a reversal from the Great Recession. In 2009, union approval bottomed out at 48%, and 42% of Americans wanted unions to have less influence while just 25% wanted them to have more.

Reality check: Americans are embracing unions at a time when few workers belong to one. Just 11% of U.S. workers — 16.5 million — were represented by unions in 2025, compared with 23% and 20.5 million workers in 1983, the first year of comparable data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

  • The most recent year included union representation for less than 7% of private-sector workers.

State of play: Workers have been trying to make up for lost time. Union election petitions filed with the National Labor Relations Board more than doubled from 2021 to 3,286 in 2024. The agency received 2,633 election petitions last year, down from the prior year's peak but still well above earlier years.

  • Americans are skeptical that today's goodwill will translate into greater strength. Just 27% expect unions to become stronger, while 39% expect them to weaken and 29% expect little change, according to the Gallup polling.
Data: Gallup Poll Social Series; Chart: Andrew Pantazi/Axios

Zoom in: Organized labor has repeatedly failed to turn Democratic control of Washington into its biggest legislative prize: rewriting federal law to make it easier for workers to join unions and to win contracts.

  • The Employee Free Choice Act, a signature priority at the start of the Obama administration, would have made it easier for workers to unionize when a majority of workers signed cards. Despite overwhelming Democratic majorities in the House and Senate, it never became law.
  • In 2021, the House passed the Protecting the Right to Organize Act, the next sweeping attempt to rewrite federal labor law, with five Republicans joining Democrats.
  • But it stalled in the Senate where Republicans and even Democratic Sens. Mark Kelly, Mark Warner and Kyrsten Sinema withheld their support.

Between the lines: President Biden leaned on executive action and appointments, creating a task force to promote organizing and pushing the NLRB to favor unionizing workers. In 2023, he became the first president to join striking workers on a picket line, standing with autoworkers in Michigan.

  • The environment has swung sharply. President Trump has used executive orders to remove collective bargaining rights for broad swaths of the federal workforce and to fire the labor board's pro-union general counsel and a Democratic board member.

The latest: House Republicans have also intensified scrutiny of union leadership, launching investigations into the United Auto Workers, United Steelworkers, the American Federation of Teachers and three railroad unions, demanding records about political activity.

The bottom line: Labor has won back popularity it lost during decades of decline, but its harder fight is turning that goodwill into bargaining power and growing its membership.

item.title: Not so fast on rate hikes, some Fed officials say
item.description:
After Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh's speech in Jackson Hole, the markets penciled in an interest rate hike for the central bank's mid-September meeting. Comments from two influential officials now throw those expectations into question.

The big picture: With August jobs and inflation data due out before a policy meeting in two weeks, the decision of whether to tighten policy appears to be on a knife-edge.

  • A meaningful contingent of Fed leadership is eager to raise interest rates to address stubbornly high inflation, while another, as Fed governor Christopher Waller put it Thursday morning, channeling John Lennon, is willing to "give disinflation a chance."
  • It's a close enough call that Warsh will likely be able to steer a decision whichever way he prefers.

Driving the news: At a Reuters newsmaker event Thursday, Waller noted two consecutive months of improving inflation data. If it continues in August reports over the coming days, he said, "I would be inclined to support" holding rates steady.

  • But if the incoming data shows "improvement has been fleeting," he is open to a rate hike, Waller added.
  • On Wednesday, New York Fed president John Williams told CNBC that "I think we have to wait and see" whether an interest rate increase is needed.
  • "There's no clear signs right now whether monetary policy is currently sufficient to make sure we bring inflation back to target in the next year or two, or whether you need to see further action to do that."

State of play: Their comments come after Warsh said that the Fed "must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective, clearly and at sufficient speed," or else they "have work to do."

  • That leaves room for a judgment call on whether that bar has been reached. Warsh has resisted hanging policy decisions on the fine details of each incoming data release, as Waller seems inclined to do.
  • CME's FedWatch tool now puts the odds of a rate hike at the meeting concluding Sept. 16 as essentially a coin flip, whereas on Wednesday, the futures market-based odds favored an increase.

Zoom in: The New York Fed president is vice chair of the policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee and has traditionally acted as part of a leadership troika, with the chairman and vice chair of the Board of Governors.

  • Traditionally, governors like Waller are reluctant to dissent from policy decisions, though that norm has dissolved in the last couple of years.
  • Three reserve bank presidents, meanwhile, dissented at the late July meeting favoring a rate hike, implying that Warsh will face internal disagreement — the "good family fight" he often speaks of — no matter which way he ultimately leans.

Of note: Waller has offered none-too-subtle criticisms of Warsh's reticent communication style. Warsh has said he wants markets to react to "the ball" of incoming data, not "the ref," or how the Fed may react to it.

  • On Thursday morning, Waller made his own addendum to that metaphor.
  • "I view myself as a home plate umpire in baseball," he said. Both the pitcher and the batter "want to play the ball, but they cannot do that until they know the umpire's strike zone," which is essentially the umpire's reaction function.
  • "If the ball goes here, it's a strike; if it goes there, it's a ball. The players don't expect the umpire to have a perfect strike zone — they just need a rough idea of its parameters and some guarantee that it won't change much on every pitch."

item.title: Top Pentagon official reaffirms Anthropic blacklist despite Lutnick comments
item.description:
Pentagon official Emil Michael on Thursday said that Anthropic is still considered a "supply chain risk," a day after Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said the company is "back on the right side."

Why it matters: The Trump administration is not entirely aligned on one of the world's leading AI labs following months of fighting over how the military can use its models.

What they're saying: "Anthropic is still a designated Supply Chain Risk at @DeptofWar and for the Defense Industrial Base. Thank you for your attention to this matter!" Michael posted on X.

Catch up quick: Lutnick told Axios' Mike Allen on the sidelines of the G20 Innovation Summit this week: "We trust Anthropic."

  • "They've done what we asked. They're back on the right side. So the answer is: Yes," Lutnick said when asked if he trusts Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei.
  • Personality differences under Amodei's leadership added fuel to the fire in a clash between the Trump administration and Anthropic earlier this year, but the company has been elevating co-founder Tom Brown's role in its relationship with the White House.

Yes, but: A federal judge in August struck down the Pentagon's blacklisting of Anthropic as a supply-chain risk, but the company is still fighting a separate Pentagon designation under a different statute in the D.C. Circuit.

The bottom line: Anthropic is not completely out of the woods with the Trump administration as Brown increasingly takes center stage.

item.title: Widespread AI outage underway
item.description:
OpenAI's ChatGPT, Anthropic's Claude, and xAI's Grok are all down Thursday morning, according to the outage company Downdetector.

Why it matters: Outages are common, but it's unusual for all three to go down at once, especially as the world increasingly relies on AI models.

  • There have also been reported issues with Google's Gemini, but the company has not issued a confirmed outage notice.

Driving the news: Anthropic's Claude dashboard is experiencing outages across Opus 4.8 and Opus 5, and says all other models "have recovered to baseline error rate."

  • ChatGPT and Codex are actively experiencing "elevated errors," according to OpenAI's dashboard.
  • Grok is "experiencing issues," according to xAI, which says it's working on the problem.

The intrigue: Microsoft Azure, which provides cloud services for all three models, is also experiencing outages, and some tech outlets have suggested Microsoft's problem may be contributing to the AI model outages.

Editor's note: This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

item.title: Gloria Steinem, feminist icon, dies at 92
item.description:
Gloria Steinem, the journalist, activist and organizer who became the most recognizable face of the U.S. women's movement, died Wednesday at 92.

The big picture: Steinem resisted being cast as feminism's singular face, but for six decades she carried its ideas into mainstream America across its second and third waves.

  • Steinem made the personal political: An illegal abortion at 22 preceded decades of fighting first to legalize abortion and then to defend that right.

Steinem died peacefully, surrounded by people who loved her at her home in New York City, according to a Thursday announcement posted from her and her foundation's Instagram accounts.

  • "Gloria's greatest gift was her ability to listen to others, to make others feel seen and heard," the announcement said.

Flashback: Steinem first drew national attention as a journalist in 1963 when she went undercover as a Playboy Bunny and exposed the job's low pay and sexist treatment.

  • Soon, she was both chronicling feminism's emerging second wave and organizing within it.

Zoom in: While attending a 1969 abortion speak-out in Greenwich Village, Steinem had what she later called a "big click" about her own abortion.

  • She joined the movement to legalize abortion before Roe v. Wade, and she lived long enough to see the Supreme Court overturn that ruling nearly 50 years later.

Steinem co-founded Ms. magazine, bringing feminist arguments about work, sex, politics, family and reproductive rights to a mass audience.

  • She also helped found the National Women's Political Caucus.
  • She took her fight to Congress, testifying for the Equal Rights Amendment in 1970, and to the American people, campaigning for its ratification.

Between the lines: She used her celebrity as a tool even as she rejected the media's tendency to reduce a diverse movement to one white spokesperson.

  • "I learned feminism largely from Black women," Steinem later told the New Yorker. For years, she traveled and spoke alongside Black feminist organizer Dorothy Pitman Hughes, who challenged racism and classism within the women's movement.

What's next: Her final memoir, "An Unexpected Life," is expected to publish later this month.

  • Her New York brownstone is also intended to remain a gathering place for social justice movements, according to Thursday's announcement.

item.title: Altman raises stakes on government scrutiny as AI advances
item.description:
CHAPEL HILL, N.C. — OpenAI CEO Sam Altman called the Trump administration's voluntary review of the company's forthcoming Astra model a "productive process" and said that closer engagement with government officials around the world will matter more as AI capabilities advance.

Why it matters: OpenAI is close to releasing Astra, the first model designated at its "critical" cyber capability level that the company says requires stronger safeguards during development and before release.

The Trump administration has developed a voluntary framework for reviewing some advanced AI models before release, including potentially giving government officials access for up to 30 days. The White House does not plan to publicly release the framework.

  • That leaves much of the government's approach opaque to the public and companies outside the process, even as leading labs participate and more powerful models are released.

Altman, in an interview with Axios, confirmed the administration reviewed Astra and noted the process is voluntary: "But we of course did it."

  • "As these models get to a quite significant level of capability, I think the importance of really doing this, closely engaging with the safety institutes in the U.S., the U.K. and elsewhere in the world, will become more important."
  • Altman called Astra "a significant step forward."

Context: Altman flew to the G20 Innovation Ministerial on Wednesday to speak with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick before an audience of commerce and technology ministers, who over two days heard the U.S. pitch on lead the world in AI.

  • During a fireside chat with Lutnick at the summit lunch, Altman said he sees OpenAI as "the pragmatic centrists … We think people need to be at the center of the economy and society and global decision-making, and that people should run the future, not AI."
  • Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, talking with Lutnick at the summit breakfast, warned against fear-driven AI messaging. "The worst outcome," he told the foreign leader, "is that you don't take advantage of it [AI], that you are left behind."
  • Huang's message prompted nods from many of the ministers in the room.

Altman, speaking with Axios, called for a "realistic" and "accurate" approach.

  • "I think doomerism — for the sake of trying to have more power, control or enforce a worldview — is really bad," he said. "I think blind optimism without an acknowledgment of the risks is also bad."

Between the lines: OpenAI and Anthropic have faced criticism that their support for some AI regulation could advantage the leading labs and make it harder for smaller competitors to keep up.

The big picture: Altman said he expected Congress to establish a "basic framework" for advanced AI after he first testified before lawmakers in 2023, but that hasn't happened.

  • "I thought at that time that Congress was going to do something," Altman told Axios.
  • He said the inaction is likely due to the pace of the technology: "People have a hard time knowing how to regulate the right things and not slow down innovation," adding that "it appears to be very hard to get Congress to do big things."

What's next: Expect OpenAI to continue releasing its models as nations grapple with safety questions.

  • "Take our word for it that we have much, much, much more capable models coming soon, and try to think about what all the impacts of that on society could be and then need to get that right," Altman said.

item.title: Brain implants fuel U.S.-China bioscience rivalry
item.description:
Brain implants like those being developed by Elon Musk's Neuralink are becoming the latest friction point in the intensifying U.S.-China rivalry in the life sciences.

Why it matters: The devices are bringing new hope to patients with strokes, Parkinson's disease and other neurological conditions. And tech billionaires have fueled advances by pouring billions into biotech startups focused on linking the brain with computers.

  • But a new national security analysis says U.S. development efforts are being overtaken by Beijing's full-court press around manufacturing, data and commercialization.
  • The consequences could extend beyond health care, affecting U.S. military capabilities and the ability to train the next generation of AI models, according to the analysis.
  • The report was produced by the National Security Commission on Emerging Biotechnology, which was created by Congress to review how biotechnology can affect national security.

State of play: Brain-computer interfaces, or BCIs, are going mainstream. Companies like Neuralink, Precision Neuroscience, Paradromics and Synchron are testing new applications, like helping to restore communication for people who have lost the ability to speak.

  • Rapid advances in artificial intelligence are reducing the time it takes to calibrate a device to a patient's brain signals and use them for functions like controlling a prosthetic part.
  • And China leveled up the field this spring, when its National Medical Products Administration issued what's thought to be the world's first commercial approval of a BCI designed to revive hand movement in people with spinal cord injuries.
  • The approval was part of a strategy that designated BCIs as a national "future industry," alongside quantum computing and 6G wireless communications systems.

The commission analysis says regulatory bottlenecks and funding concerns are drying up the U.S. pipeline for BCIs and shifting the playing field in China's favor, noting that new treatments for neurological conditions take an average of more than 11 years to reach approval.

  • It calls for the Food and Drug Administration to develop a clearer pathway for bringing implants to market, and for the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services to come up with a way to pay for devices once they're through regulatory approvals.
  • "China is moving strategic technologies like BCI faster than the United States can," Sen. Todd Young (R-Ind.), the chair of the national security commission, tells Axios.
  • "Our government needs a coordinated biotechnology strategy to promote U.S. innovation and commercialization of what promises to be a truly revolutionary platform technology for health and national security."

Between the lines: BCIs are another example of how technology is outpacing regulation — and posing thorny ethical and privacy issues.

  • There's the basic question of who controls the device and data, and whether privacy laws like the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act even apply.
  • Giving patients more control over their data may require new laws or regulations that could limit developers' ability to improve algorithms that decode brain signals, the Government Accountability Office has noted.
  • But more consumer autonomy could provide safeguards that extend beyond medical settings and protect against data being accessed to make insurance or workplace decisions, or to study how people subconsciously respond to advertising or other messages.
  • China currently has no neural-data-specific privacy or security regulations, per the commission analysis.

Reality check: Brain implants remain a work in progress. Many fail within their first year, and experts say manufacturing improvements like new materials, coatings and batteries could address signal degradation and extend power life.

  • It's also difficult to recruit patients for clinical trials who have profound disabilities but still are healthy enough to withstand brain surgery.

What we're watching: Whether brain implants are included in the Trump administration's RAPID program — a joint effort between FDA and CMS to expedite Medicare coverage of certain "breakthrough" devices.

  • Longer term, BCIs could be adapted for nonmedical purposes, like controlling swarms of drones through operators' thoughts.

  • Rapid advances in artificial intelligence are reducing the time it takes to calibrate a device to a patient's brain signals and use them for functions like controlling a prosthetic part.
  • And China leveled up the field this spring, when its National Medical Products Administration issued what's thought to be the world's first commercial approval of a BCI designed to revive hand movement in people with spinal cord injuries.
  • The approval was part of a strategy that designated BCIs as a national "future industry," alongside quantum computing and 6G wireless communications systems.

The commission analysis says regulatory bottlenecks and funding concerns are drying up the U.S. pipeline for BCIs and shifting the playing field in China's favor, noting that new treatments for neurological conditions take an average of more than 11 years to reach approval.

  • It calls for the Food and Drug Administration to develop a clearer pathway for bringing implants to market, and for the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services to come up with a way to pay for devices once they're through regulatory approvals.
  • "China is moving strategic technologies like BCI faster than the United States can," Sen. Todd Young (R-Ind.), the chair of the national security commission, tells Axios.
  • "Our government needs a coordinated biotechnology strategy to promote U.S. innovation and commercialization of what promises to be a truly revolutionary platform technology for health and national security."

Between the lines: BCIs are another example of how technology is outpacing regulation — and posing thorny ethical and privacy issues.

  • There's the basic question of who controls the device and data, and whether privacy laws like the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act even apply.
  • Giving patients more control over their data may require new laws or regulations that could limit developers' ability to improve algorithms that decode brain signals, the Government Accountability Office has noted.
  • But more consumer autonomy could provide safeguards that extend beyond medical settings and protect against data being accessed to make insurance or workplace decisions, or to study how people subconsciously respond to advertising or other messages.
  • China currently has no neural-data-specific privacy or security regulations, per the commission analysis.

Reality check: Brain implants remain a work in progress. Many fail within their first year, and experts say manufacturing improvements like new materials, coatings and batteries could address signal degradation and extend power life.

  • It's also difficult to recruit patients for clinical trials who have profound disabilities but still are healthy enough to withstand brain surgery.

What we're watching: Whether brain implants are included in the Trump administration's RAPID program — a joint effort between FDA and CMS to expedite Medicare coverage of certain "breakthrough" devices.

  • Longer term, BCIs could be adapted for nonmedical purposes, like controlling swarms of drones through operators' thoughts.

item.title: Markets can't ignore the war anymore
item.description:
Oil prices are heading back toward $100 a barrel, and, perhaps more crucially, the price of diesel fuel futures is now sitting at an all-time high. 

Why it matters: Investors are starting to recognize that higher oil prices from the Iran war aren't something they can continue to ignore.

The big picture: Higher energy prices are showing up across the economy, driving up costs for companies, regular people and even governments around the world that are now facing higher borrowing rates.

  • The rising price of energy is a big factor pushing bond yields higher and worrying policymakers in the U.S. and the rest of the developed world.

Catch up quick: After falling off initial early war highs, oil prices started rising in July. At the time, attacks on commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz reignited fighting, and President Trump said the "memorandum of understanding" the two countries had signed weeks before was "over."

State of play: Over the past few days, tensions have intensified.

  • The price of a barrel of Brent crude oil, the global benchmark, was trading at $95 on Wednesday afternoon, up from the low $80s a month ago.

By the numbers: The yield on the 10-year Treasury — a benchmark for mortgages and other loans — was hovering at around 4.8% Wednesday, after touching its highest level in nearly three years.

Follow the money: Government bond yields around the world are also at multiyear highs.

  • The U.K.'s 10-year gilt hit its highest level since 2008; Germany's long bond rose to its highest since 2011. And the government bonds of Japan, an importer of oil vulnerable to energy price shocks, touched their highest level since 1996.
  • Stocks have moved basically sideways over the past week.

How it works: The rise in oil prices is driving up inflation expectations, as people expect higher energy costs to drive up both the cost of making things and the cost of moving those things from place to place.

  • That's impacting government bond yields, as investors demand more interest to compensate for inflation eating away at the value of their money.
  • Those inflation expectations are also affecting stock valuations, some analysts believe — expectations for future earnings don't look as high once you take higher inflation into account.

Zoom out: The correlation between the price of oil and the 10-year Treasury yield is close to its strongest in five years, per an analysis from Morgan Stanley. (That means they're moving up together.)

  • The stock/oil correlation is nearly its most negative. (Stocks move down, while oil moves up.)

Yes, but: Government bond yields are moving up for other reasons as well — including unsustainable deficits, geopolitical uncertainty and even the AI boom, as we've written about before.

  • The relationship between stocks and oil can be murky. Certainly the war is driving up share prices in sectors like energy.

Catch up quick: The initial shock of the U.S.-Iran war clobbered stocks back in early March, but they bounced back — partly after the two sides reached a ceasefire agreement in June.

  • Energy prices also retreated as it became clear that other forces — especially China importing less oil — were keeping them in check.

The bottom line: Those days may now be behind us. "For global markets the oil pain has become too great to ignore," investor Bob Elliott wrote in a note Wednesday morning.

Bonus Chart:

The market for diesel fuel is feeling the energy squeeze most acutely. Diesel is a key input for just about anything grown or transported through the U.S.

And the price of benchmark diesel futures is sitting at an all-time high of $4.73 per gallon.

Data: FactSet; Note: NY Harbor ultra-low sulfur; Chart: Emily Peck/Axios

item.title: Historic first: Older adults now outnumber the youngest children for the first time
item.description:
Data: U.S. Census Bureau, International Database; Chart: Noah Bressner/Axios

People 65 and older now outnumber children ages 5 and younger worldwide for the first time in recorded history, according to a new report by the U.S. Census.

Why it matters: A global plunge in fertility — demographers' term for the number of children being born — and increased longevity are creating a demographic inversion that's projected to deepen for decades.

  • It's a trend that's shifting the historic balance between working-age people and older adults.

By the numbers: The scale and speed of the shift as the youngest Baby Boomers move toward their mid-60s are striking. They reflect the scope of the challenge in caring for the elderly and maintaining programs such as Social Security in the U.S., an Axios analysis of the Census data found.

  • More than 71% of the world's population lived in countries with fertility rates at or below the roughly 2.1-births-per-woman replacement level in 2023.
  • That's up from 45% in 2013. The Census says the world reached that tipping point much earlier than demographers expected just a decade ago.
  • The population of those 65+ is projected to grow from 852 million in 2025 to 2 billion in 2060.

Stunning stat: That increase would account for about 55% of all net global population growth over that period, according to an Axios calculation using Census projections.

  • The world's total population is projected to rise from 8.13 billion to 10.23 billion by 2060.

State of play: The low-birth era has spread far beyond wealthy countries.

  • China and India — the world's two most populous countries — now have fertility rates below the roughly 2.1-births-per-woman replacement level, the Census report says.
  • Bangladesh, Mexico and Vietnam are among the most populous countries to fall below replacement-level births since 2013.

Zoom in: In many countries with low birth rates, the decline creates what the report calls a "fertility trap."

  • Smaller younger generations follow larger older ones, accelerating the overall aging of a population and, in some places, eventual population decline.
  • That means fewer potential workers and caregivers supporting growing older populations — putting pressure on pensions, health systems and long-term care.

The intrigue: The U.S. ranked as the 48th-oldest country out of 227 in 2025, with 18.9% of its population age 65 or older.

  • By 2060, the U.S. share of older adults is projected to climb to 23.4%, but its global aging rank is predicted to fall to 110th because other countries are aging much faster.
Data: U.S. Census Bureau, International Database, 2023, Axios calculations; Chart: Russell Contreras/Axios

Zoom out: Europe remains the world's oldest region, but the biggest numerical shift in aging is elsewhere.

  • Asia's 65+ population is projected to surge from 487 million to 1.24 billion from 2025 to 2060 — accounting for roughly two-thirds of the global increase.
  • Africa remains by far the youngest region, but its older population is projected to more than quadruple from 60 million to 249 million — surpassing Europe's 214 million by 2060.
  • Globally, the share of people 65+ is projected to nearly double from 10.5% to 19.6% by 2060.

Yes, but: A nation's rising percentage of seniors isn't necessarily a catastrophe.

  • Longer lives represent one of the great achievements of the past century: fewer deaths in infancy and midlife, and more people surviving into old age.
  • Older people are less likely to commit crime and many can remain in the workforce, help fill labor shortages and contribute through caregiving and volunteering.

Between the lines: The demographic shift could force societies to rethink old age as an economic asset rather than simply a cost, Census report contributor Andrew Scott said.

  • He argues in the report that preventive health, longer working lives and age-friendly jobs could turn longer lifespans into healthier, more economically engaged years.

item.title: Alaska seeks oil revival while grappling with a warming future
item.description:
EXIT GLACIER, Alaska — America's 49th state is a study in contrasts: Rapidly melting glaciers like this one attract tourists, while the oil industry underpinning its economy is getting a fresh boost from Washington after decades of decline.

Why it matters: Few places put the causes and consequences of global warming in such proximity, making Alaska a vivid window into the world's reliance on fossil fuels as climate impacts mount.

Driving the news: "Alaska is a powerhouse," Energy Secretary Chris Wright said last week in Anchorage at the state oil and gas trade group's annual conference, according to Alaska News Source.

  • "I think you could have an incredible several years, several decades coming with just some common sense policies to set Alaskans free."

State of play: Alaska has emerged as perhaps the Trump administration's biggest geographic focus for expanding U.S. oil and gas development, with the government pushing new leasing, easier permitting, Arctic drilling and a massive natural gas pipeline.

  • A major new North Slope oil field started producing in May, and another is expected to begin producing in 2029.
  • Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) told Axios this moment is a "second wind" for the state's oil industry.

The big picture: No offense to Texas, but everything is actually bigger in Alaska.

  • It's more than double the size of Texas and has more coastline than all other states combined.
  • It ranks near the top for both proven oil and gas reserves in the nation, and it has the largest icefield wholly contained in the U.S., the Harding Icefield, which feeds Exit Glacier.

Reality check: Alaska's heyday as a top oil powerhouse is likely behind it. Its oil production has been declining since the late 1980s, and projects underway aren't expected to restore anything close to that.

Friction point: Some of Washington's efforts are facing hurdles.

  • The Interior Department's June lease sale in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge, a vast wilderness home to polar bears, caribou and hundreds of bird species, generated little industry interest. A separate sale for new drilling in Cook Inlet near Anchorage received zero bids.
  • An Interior Department spokesperson described the wildlife refuge auction as "a success for this frontier area," and pointed to a record-breaking March lease sale elsewhere in Alaska's North Slope.

Zoom in: The roughly $50 billion effort to pipe natural gas 800 miles from the North Slope to the Kenai Peninsula for export to Asian markets is struggling to move forward.

  • Wright called it his "number one" energy infrastructure priority earlier this year.
  • But last week, he said: "I'm disappointed that I'm sitting here right now and we're not talking about shovels in the ground," Alaska News reported.
  • Jason Bordoff, founding director of Columbia University's Center on Global Energy Policy, who recently visited Alaska's northernmost regions, called the economics of the project "terrible."

Inside the room: Or more aptly: next to the glacier. Signs along the hiking trail at Exit Glacier tell visitors how much this glacier has retreated dating back to the late 1880s; the most recent sign is from 2010.

  • Its retreat has accelerated in recent decades due to human-caused warming, according to Albin Wells, who researches the topic at the University of Zurich.
  • The seven glaciers near the ski town of Girdwood are all likely to vanish or be vastly reduced within 75 years, Wells said.
  • One of our guides near Girdwood, describing how dramatically the glaciers had changed during his lifetime, said he avoids the term "climate change" because of its polarizing politics.
Axios' Amy Harder, on Aug. 16, standing at the most recent sign showing where the Exit Glacier, pictured in the foreground, reached in 2010. Photo courtesy of Amy Harder/Axios

Between the lines: The changes go far beyond glaciers: Thawing permafrost and disappearing sea ice are destabilizing land and accelerating erosion along parts of Alaska's coast.

Follow the money: One of the nation's fastest-warming states remains deeply reliant on oil and gas.

  • Decades of oil wealth helped build the Alaska Permanent Fund, which now provides more unrestricted state revenue than current oil and gas revenues do — as well as an annual dividend for residents.

What we're watching: With energy security demanding attention amid the ongoing Iran war, climate change may be on the back burner, Bordoff said, "but it is going to come back in a nonlinear way because of the impacts we're seeing."

Sign up here for Axios' Future of Energy newsletter.

item.title: House Democrats erupt into infighting over leadership power play
item.description:
House Democratic leaders are trying to flex some muscle this week after two members defected on a key procedural vote. It's stoking fury among members across the political spectrum.

Why it matters: The blowup offers a preview of the chaos that party leaders could face in January if they take back the House majority.

  • Meanwhile, an effort to give House Democratic leaders more tools to keep their members in line next year is falling flat among rank-and-file members.
  • "It'll be dead by next week," predicted one senior House Democrat, speaking to Axios on the condition of anonymity to comment candidly on the maneuver.

Driving the news: Reps. Jared Golden (D-Maine) and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D-Wash.) touched off a flurry of anger from fellow Democrats on Tuesday by helping Republicans pass a procedural measure known as a "rule."

  • The measure allowed for House votes on a slew of measures, including a GOP resolution denouncing socialism and a bipartisan bill co-led by Golden to shield lobstermen from regulations protecting whales.
  • House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) and his deputies were upset that Golden and Gluesenkamp Perez defected without a heads-up.
  • They put out a rare joint statement accusing the two centrists of a "significant breach of trust" that "necessitates a serious response."

Several proposed responses have been floated behind the scenes, lawmakers and aides told Axios.

  • Some members have suggested kicking both members off of their committees, or at least removing Gluesenkamp Perez from the powerful House Appropriations Committee.
  • Others have pitched a broader change to caucus rules requiring members to show up to key votes, stick with party leadership on rule votes and pay their dues to the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee.
  • Under this proposal, members who fail to adhere to those standards would not be members of the caucus in "good standing," which could in turn lead to them losing out on prime committee appointments.

Yes, but: Several senior Congressional Progressive Caucus members told Axios they would strongly oppose such a rules change.

  • Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.), the deputy chair of the Progressive Caucus, told Axios: "Something like that, I don't think will be ... supported."
  • "It could be used against everyone," she said. "I think it's really important that we ... defeat it."
  • Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.), the Progressive Caucus' chair emerita, told Axios the rules change is "not going to fly."

Between the lines: Progressives are "furious" about the proposal, said the senior House Democrat who spoke to Axios anonymously, in part because many moderates in swing districts are exempt from paying DCCC dues.

  • "The feeling is they hold CPC to a different standard," the senior lawmaker said.
  • The rules change was a topic of furious conversation among CPC members on the House floor Wednesday afternoon, sources told Axios.

What they're saying: House Democratic Caucus chair Pete Aguilar (D-Calif.) told Axios "it's up to the caucus ... to decide if they want to vote on a rule and what that rule looks like."

  • "Any member of the caucus can read the rules that govern the meetings and ... offer a rule change whenever it's appropriate," he said.
  • Aguilar declined to state a personal position on whether the rules should be changed, saying he will "share it when it's appropriate."

Some centrists, meanwhile, said the idea of removing Golden or Gluesenkamp Perez from committees would be a slap in the face to their wing of the party.

  • They noted there have been more than a dozen instances in the past several congressional sessions in which Democrats — including progressives — broke with party leaders on rule votes but faced no repercussions.
  • One centrist House Democrat complained that "nothing happened" to a group of progressive "Squad" members who broke with leadership on a rule vote in 2022.
  • A Progressive Caucus source pushed back on that, however, noting that they voted against a Democratic rule rather than for a Republican one as Golden and Gluesenkamp Perez did.

"If they're going to apply it only to us, hell yeah that would be a big problem for everybody," battleground district Rep. Vicente Gonzalez (D-Texas) told Axios.

  • He added: "They can't single us out. We have tough districts. In fact, if anybody gets a pass it should be front-liners defending seats that, if it weren't for us, the Republicans would have."
  • Several moderates said they want assurances from leadership that, if Golden and Gluesenkamp Perez are punished, the standard will be applied equally to all members going forward.

The bottom line: Many lawmakers speculated that this episode was leadership's way of trying to signal a new, more authoritative style in anticipation of taking back the House majority.

  • The centrist House Democrat who spoke anonymously said of Jeffries: "He's just laying the groundwork."

Editor's note: This story has been updated to clarify a comment from a centrist Democrat about a rule vote in 2022.

  • Others have pitched a broader change to caucus rules requiring members to show up to key votes, stick with party leadership on rule votes and pay their dues to the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee.
  • Under this proposal, members who fail to adhere to those standards would not be members of the caucus in "good standing," which could in turn lead to them losing out on prime committee appointments.

Yes, but: Several senior Congressional Progressive Caucus members told Axios they would strongly oppose such a rules change.

  • Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.), the deputy chair of the Progressive Caucus, told Axios: "Something like that, I don't think will be ... supported."
  • "It could be used against everyone," she said. "I think it's really important that we ... defeat it."
  • Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.), the Progressive Caucus' chair emerita, told Axios the rules change is "not going to fly."

Between the lines: Progressives are "furious" about the proposal, said the senior House Democrat who spoke to Axios anonymously, in part because many moderates in swing districts are exempt from paying DCCC dues.

  • "The feeling is they hold CPC to a different standard," the senior lawmaker said.
  • The rules change was a topic of furious conversation among CPC members on the House floor Wednesday afternoon, sources told Axios.

What they're saying: House Democratic Caucus chair Pete Aguilar (D-Calif.) told Axios "it's up to the caucus ... to decide if they want to vote on a rule and what that rule looks like."

  • "Any member of the caucus can read the rules that govern the meetings and ... offer a rule change whenever it's appropriate," he said.
  • Aguilar declined to state a personal position on whether the rules should be changed, saying he will "share it when it's appropriate."

Some centrists, meanwhile, said the idea of removing Golden or Gluesenkamp Perez from committees would be a slap in the face to their wing of the party.

  • They noted there have been more than a dozen instances in the past several congressional sessions in which Democrats — including progressives — broke with party leaders on rule votes but faced no repercussions.
  • One centrist House Democrat complained that "nothing happened" to a group of progressive "Squad" members who broke with leadership on a rule vote in 2022.
  • A Progressive Caucus source pushed back on that, however, noting that they voted against a Democratic rule rather than for a Republican one as Golden and Gluesenkamp Perez did.

"If they're going to apply it only to us, hell yeah that would be a big problem for everybody," battleground district Rep. Vicente Gonzalez (D-Texas) told Axios.

  • He added: "They can't single us out. We have tough districts. In fact, if anybody gets a pass it should be front-liners defending seats that, if it weren't for us, the Republicans would have."
  • Several moderates said they want assurances from leadership that, if Golden and Gluesenkamp Perez are punished, the standard will be applied equally to all members going forward.

The bottom line: Many lawmakers speculated that this episode was leadership's way of trying to signal a new, more authoritative style in anticipation of taking back the House majority.

  • The centrist House Democrat who spoke anonymously said of Jeffries: "He's just laying the groundwork."

Editor's note: This story has been updated to clarify a comment from a centrist Democrat about a rule vote in 2022.

item.title: Witkoff meets powerful UAE official amid crackdown on Iran
item.description:
White House Envoy Steve Witkoff met last weekend with the national security adviser of the United Arab Emirates to discuss next steps on Iran, according to two sources with knowledge of the meeting.

Why it matters: The talks, which weren't announced by the White House and haven't been reported until now, took place amid the Trump administration's push to reopen the Strait of Hormuz while choking Iran economically. Witkoff met with Sheikh Tahnoon Bin Zayed al Nahyan (TBZ) on the Mediterranean island of Sardinia.

  • The UAE has been the key partner in the U.S.-led operation to reopen and guide oil tankers through the strait. It is also critical to the success of the U.S. economic pressure campaign against Iran.
  • TBZ is one of the UAE's most powerful figures: He is the brother of President Mohammed bin Zayed, the country's national security adviser and deputy ruler of Abu Dhabi, and oversees the UAE's vast investment and technology interests.
  • Witkoff and TBZ brainstormed next steps in the Iranian crisis and discussed other issues, the sources said.
  • The White House didn't respond to a request for comment.

Driving the news: The meeting took place several days after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced "Operation Economic Outcast" — a vow to level punishing sanctions on countries and entities that do business with the Islamic Republic.

  • Bessent spoke to TBZ ahead of the announcement, according to a source with knowledge of the call.
  • On the day of Witkoff's meeting with TBZ, the Treasury Department moved to cut off the UAE branches of Egypt's Banque Misr from the U.S. financial system over its business with Iran. The proposed action would block the bank's dollar transactions.
  • The UAE central bank said it would conduct an "urgent examination" of the transactions that the Egyptian bank's branches had with Iran.

Zoom in: Several days before the Trump administration's sanctions announcement, the UAE decided to halt all trade, commercial exchange and financial transactions with Iran.

  • It was a dramatic move because the UAE — primarily Dubai — had served as a major trading and re-export hub for Iran. Trade between the countries in 2024 reached $28 billion.
  • A second source with knowledge of the matter said Emirati officials told the Trump administration that any economic pressure campaign against Iran must include all key countries that trade with the Islamic Republic in order for it to be effective.

Behind the scenes: The upcoming Trump administration secondary sanctions against Iran were a factor in the UAE's decision, but not the main reason, according to two sources with knowledge of the issue.

  • On Aug. 11, an Iranian delegation visited Abu Dhabi for low-key diplomatic talks with Emirati officials, sources said.
  • During the talks, the sources said, the Iranians said they wanted to deescalate and improve relations — after Iran had fired thousands of missiles and drones at the UAE during the war.
  • The Iranians even asked the UAE for help securing food and medicine, and urged the Emiratis not to cooperate with U.S. sanctions — a request that was immediately rejected, the sources said.
  • But in the following few days, the IRGC intensified its attacks on UAE national oil company tankers that tried to transit through the Strait of Hormuz.
  • The Emiratis were furious and decided to suspend all business with Iran, the sources said.

What to watch: Secretary of State Marco Rubio earlier this week instructed all U.S. embassies around the world to send an official diplomatic demarche about Operation Economic Outcast to the most senior level of their host governments, U.S. officials said.

  • U.S. embassies were told to demand that countries "immediately and systematically" sever all trade with Iran and identify illicit Iranian business activity.
  • The U.S. demarche stressed that countries, companies and individuals that continue doing business with Iran risk being sanctioned and disconnected from the dollar system, the U.S. officials said.
  • One of the officials said a special message was sent to U.S. diplomatic posts in Abu Dhabi, Muscat, Hong Kong, Doha, London, Berlin and several Central Asian capitals. The missive instructed them to demand that their host governments shut down all branches of Iran's Melli and Saderat banks that are affiliated with the IRGC.

What's next: The Trump administration is working to set up an interagency task force to coordinate the implementation and enforcement of the economic pressure campaign against Iran, the U.S. official said.

item.title: The $1 Trump coins are here. Why spending them is legal but tricky
item.description:
The U.S. Mint began selling $1 Trump coins Wednesday.

Why it matters: The Trump coin sits in a rare middle ground: The Mint is promoting it as a collectible, but under federal law, it has a face value of $1 and can be used as real money.

Driving the news: The U.S. Mint says the Trump coins are now "in circulation, so check your pocket change."

  • The coins can be purchased in 25-coin rolls for $61 and 100-coin bags for $154.50.
  • The U.S. Mint's website says the coins have "circulating finishes but have never been placed into circulation. However, they may be still used as legal tender."

The big picture: Trump's coin has raised legal questions over whether a sitting president can appear on U.S. money.

Why the Trump coin is "legal tender"

"Legal tender" refers to U.S. money that can pay debts, taxes, dues and public charges, according to federal law.

  • The U.S. Mint deems the $1 Trump coin legal tender with a face value of $1, regardless of what a collector pays for it.

Yes, but: Legal tender doesn't guarantee every store will accept Trump coins. Federal law generally lets private businesses decide what forms of payment they'll accept.

  • Americans have been reluctant to spend $1 coins.
  • The Sacagawea dollar from the early 2000s struggled despite a multimillion-dollar marketing campaign, and the government stopped circulating presidential $1 coins in 2011 due to low demand.

Debate over Trump coin as currency

Catch up quick: Since the Trump coin was announced, questions have emerged about its design and legality because some federal laws restrict living people's portraits on U.S. coins.

  • The Presidential $1 Coin Act of 2005 permits only $1 coins honoring deceased presidents issued under that presidential series and the Circulating Collectible Coin Redesign Act of 2020 prohibits any portraits of living people on the "tails" side of a coin.

The other side: The Treasury Department argued in October 2025 that the coin can be made because the CCCRA does allow for "designs emblematic of the United States semiquincentennial."

  • In July, a Treasury spokesperson pointed Axios to an Independent article reporting that the U.S. Mint had researched whether developing the coin would violate the law.

Case in point: Calvin Coolidge, the 30th president, appeared alongside George Washington on a 1926 half-dollar celebrating America's 150th anniversary.

  • The law authorizing the coin specifically said it "shall be legal tender in any payment to the amount of their face value."
  • Although they sold for $1 apiece, their value was 50 cents.

The bottom line: The Trump $1 coin is real money, but that doesn't mean it can be spent everywhere.

Go deeper: 5 changes Trump could make to U.S. currency

item.title: Nearly 9 in 10 Americans report widespread government corruption after Trump's return
item.description:
Data: Gallup; Chart: Avery Lotz/Axios

Americans' perceptions of government corruption have hit a 20-year high following President Trump's return to office, a new Gallup survey found.

Why it matters: The results signal a deepening crisis of confidence in the federal government as trust in U.S. institutions already hovers near an all-time low.

By the numbers: 89% of U.S. adults say government corruption is widespread, Gallup found.

  • That's a 10-point increase from last year and well above the 72%–79% range between 2010 and 2025.

Democrats are driving most of the rise, jumping to 91% this year after sitting at 76% during the first year of Trump's term.

  • In 2024, when President Biden was still in office, 57% of Democrats said government corruption was widespread.
  • About 90% of independents think corruption is widespread, up 12 points since 2024.

Between the lines: Trump raked in more than $2.2 billion in the first year of his second term.

  • In 2024, he reported making about $600 million. A substantial share of Trump's income comes from non-traditional business holdings, like his cryptocurrency business.
  • He faced criticism after an investment firm tied to the United Arab Emirates bought almost half of his main crypto firm, prmopting accusations of potential foreign influence over U.S. policy.
  • He's also making money from a new plan to offer early access to his Truth Social posts, which can move markets.

Zoom out: Congressional lawmakers have repeatedly called out what they say are conflicts of interests.

  • Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) released a report in November that concluded Trump and his family significantly benefitted from rolling back crypto regulations designed to protect Americans from fraud and scams.
  • Democrats have also criticized the president for accepting lavish gifts, including a $400 million Qatari jet.
  • It's also not just the president — congressional lawmakers have faced growing scrutiny for making head-turning sums trading stocks while in office.

What they're saying: "President Trump has launched an all-out war on fraud across the entire federal government, holding criminals accountable and saving taxpayers billions of dollars," White House spokesman Davis Ingle said in an emailed statement.

  • "The Democrats in Congress have refused to do anything to stop waste, fraud, and abuse in our government."

Zoom in: Republicans have held a much steadier view of government corruption.

  • About eight in 10 say corruption is widespread, relatively on par with 2024 levels, when 87% said the same.
  • Republicans' consistent reading suggests this feeling is widespread regardless of which political party is in power.

The big picture: While citizens in many developed nations feel their governments are becoming less corrupt, Americans are experiencing the exact opposite trend.

  • Among the 38 member countries in the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development, the median level of perceived government corruption has fallen from 69% in 2009 to below 60% since 2022.
  • For the first time ever, the U.S. now tops perceived corruption ratings by comparison to the other countries in the OECD. Since 2023, just four other countries that Gallup has surveyed have scored higher than the U.S., including Lebanon, Peru, Ghana and Nigeria.
  • The data for 2026 isn't complete because Gallup conducts their polling on a country-by-country basis over the year, so that massive gap could grow wider this year.

Methodology: Gallup surveyed at least 1,000 Americans every year since 2005 to reach these results. It also surveyed between 500 and more than 3,000 people in other countries to measure sentiment across the other OECD countries. Go deeper: Trump's profits irk Americans as Dems test anti-corruption message
